Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 1:

Surat al-Mu'minun

(Makkiyyah, and it is one hundred and nineteen verses according to the Basrans, and one hundred and eighteen verses according to the Kufans.)

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded.﴾ Al-falah (success): attaining one's aim and being saved from what is disliked. It has also been said: remaining in goodness. Al-ifla (causing to succeed) is entering into that, like al-ibshar (entering into good tidings), which is entering into glad tidings. It may also come transitively in the sense of causing someone to enter into it, and the reading of the one who read it in the passive voice (uflihu, "they are made to succeed") is based on this. The word "qad" (certainly) here is for affirming the occurrence of what was already expected to occur, not for announcing what is expected to be announced, since what is expected of the state of the believers is that success be established for them, not merely the announcement of that. So the meaning is: they have achieved every good and been saved from every harm, in accordance with what was expected of their state, for their faith and the righteous deeds that branch from it are among the causes of success by the necessity of the generous promise. Except that if by ifla is meant the actual entry into the success which is not realized except in the Hereafter, then the announcement of it in the past form is to indicate its certain realization, by treating it as established. And if what is meant is that they are in a state that necessarily entails it, then the past form is in its proper place. It was also read "aflahu" (with the plural verb form changed), as an indefinite and explanatory construction, or as in "akaluni al-baraghith" (the fleas ate me). It was read "aflahu" with a single damma, dispensing with the waw, as in the verse of one who said:

"Wa law anna al-atibba' kana hawli..." (And if only the physicians were around me...)

The meaning of "the believers" here is either: those who affirm what is known by necessity to be part of the religion of our Prophet ﷺ, namely the Oneness of God (tawhid), prophethood, resurrection, recompense and their like. In that case, His saying, ﴿Those who are humble in their prayer﴾, and what is conjoined to it, are qualifying attributes that specify them. Or it means those who also perform its branches (furu'), as the attribution of prayer to them indicates. In that case the attributes are either clarifying or praising attributes for them, according to how the meanings mentioned within the scope of the relative clause are considered, together with faith, in summary or in detail, as has passed at the beginning of (Surat al-Baqarah).

Khushu' (humility, submissiveness) means fear and abasement, that is: they are fearful of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, abased before Him, keeping their gazes fixed on their places of prostration (masajid).

It is narrated that "he ﷺ, when he prayed, would raise his gaze towards the sky. When this verse was revealed, he directed his gaze towards his place of prostration. He saw a worshipper playing with his beard, and said: 'If the heart of this one were humble, his limbs would be humble.'"

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 3:

﴿And those who from idle talk﴾ i.e., from words and deeds that do not concern them.

(p-124) ﴿turn away﴾ i.e., at all times, as the noun indicating continuity signifies. This includes their turning away from it during their prayer, as an initial inclusion. The basis of their turning away from it is the state of that which calls for turning away from it, not merely being occupied with earnestness in matters of religion, as some have said, for that might give the impression that idle talk itself contains nothing that restrains them from engaging in it. Turning away is more eloquent than saying "they do not indulge," in terms of the ways of making the sentence nominal. And the building of the judgment upon the pronoun, the expression of it by the noun, the fronting of the relative clause before it, and the placing of turning away in the position of abandonment, all serve to show their distance from it entirely, directly, causally, inclinationally and presentially, since its original state is to be in a different dimension from theirs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 4:

﴿And those who are active in paying zakah﴾. He described them with this after describing them with humility (khushu') in prayer, to indicate that they have reached the furthest extent in carrying out acts of worship, both physical and financial, and in avoiding what is forbidden and everything else that bears on manliness (muru'ah) to shun, and to place the turning away from idle talk (ial-i'rad) between the two, for its complete connection to humility in prayer. And zakah (zakah, obligatory almsgiving) is a verbal noun (masdar), because it is the matter issuing from the doer, not the place where it occurs. The meaning of the verb (fi'l) has already been verified in the explanation of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿But if you do not, and you will never be able to﴾ [2:24]. It is also permissible that by it is meant the object itself (al-'ayn), on the assumption of an omitted noun (al-mudaf).

﴿And those who guard their private parts﴾ restrain them. The exception in His saying ﴿except from their spouses﴾ (istithna', exception) is taken from the negation of release that the word "guarding" implies. That is, they do not release them toward anyone except their spouses. This indicates that their sexual drive urges them toward what is obviously forbidden, and that they guard it from fulfilling what it demands, and by this complete chastity is achieved. It is permissible for "ʿalā" (on, upon) to mean "min" (from), and al-Farrā' (the grammarian) held this view, as in His saying ﴿when they take the measure from people﴾. That is: they guard their private parts from everyone except their spouses. It has also been said that the phrase is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the pronoun in "guarding." That is: they guard them in all circumstances, except when they are governing or managing their spouses. It has also been said that it is connected to an omitted element indicated by ﴿not blameworthy﴾, as if it were said: they are blamed for every intimate contact, except with what is permitted to them, for they are then not blameworthy. Taking "guarding" as restricted to them would mean: they guard their private parts for their spouses, not transgressing beyond them. Then it would be said: they are not guarding except for them, as emphasis upon emphasis, an artificial strain upon an artificial strain.

﴿or what their right hands possess﴾, that is, their concubines. He expressed them with "mā" (what) by treating them as non-rational beings because of their status as owned property, or because of their femininity, which indicates the intended meaning. His saying ﴿for they are not blameworthy﴾ is a justification for what the exception implies, namely that they do not guard their private parts from them. That is: they are not blameworthy for not guarding them from those women.

**﴿So whoever seeks beyond that﴾**, beyond the broad limit mentioned, which is four free wives and as many slave women as he wishes.

**﴿then those are the transgressors﴾**, those who are complete in transgression and who go to its utmost extent. There is nothing in it that definitively indicates the prohibition of *mut'ah* (temporary marriage), as related from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, for he said: she is not his wife, so she must not be lawful for him. As for [the claim] that she is not his wife, it is because the two do not inherit from each other by *ijma'* (consensus). Had she been his wife, inheritance would have occurred, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave﴾. So she must not be lawful, based on His saying: ﴿except from their wives﴾. This is because they may say that she is a wife of his in a general sense. As for the claim that every wife inherits, they do not concede it. As for what has been said: if it is meant that had she been a wife during life it would not benefit, and if it is meant after death, then the implication is denied, so it has no established meaning. Yes, if it were reversed, it would have some basis. (p-125)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 8:

﴿And those who are, for their trusts (amanat) and their covenant, ever-watchful﴾ — concerning what they are entrusted with and what they pledge, whether in regard to the rights of the Truth (God) or the rights of creation. ﴿Ever-watchful﴾ means: they stand over these and guard them, acting in the way of rectification. It is also recited as "li-amanatihim" (singular).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 9:

﴿And those who are over their prayers﴾ (that are prescribed upon them) ﴿guard them carefully﴾ (yuhafizun): they are constant in them and perform them at their appointed times. The verb here is in the present tense (yuhafizun) because of what prayer contains of renewal and repetition, and this is the secret of its being put in the plural (ṣalawāt, "prayers"). There is no repetition in it, since humility (khushu') in prayer is other than guarding it (al-muhafaza), and their separation (in the verse) is to indicate that each of them is an independent virtue in its own right. Had they been mentioned together, it might have been imagined that the combination of humility and guarding (in prayer) is a single virtue.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 10:

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the believers, in consideration of their being characterized by the qualities that have been mentioned. The choice of this demonstrative over a pronoun is to signal that they are distinguished by these qualities from others, and that they are placed in the position of one who is indicated by a sensory pointing; and the sense of distance contained in it serves to announce the loftiness of their rank and the remoteness of their degree in excellence and nobility. That is: those who are described with the sublime attributes mentioned.

﴿They are the inheritors﴾ That is: they are the most deserving of being named inheritors, above all others who have inherited the desirable wealth and treasures and their noblest things.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 11:

﴿Those who inherit the Firdaws﴾ is an explanation of what they inherit, and a specification of the inheritance after its generality, and an elaboration of it after its vagueness, to magnify its status and elevate its station. It is a metaphor for their deserving the Firdaws by their deeds, as the generous promise requires, for the sake of emphasis on it. It has also been said: they inherit from the disbelievers their dwellings therein, since the disbelievers forfeited them for themselves, because God, exalted is He, created for every person a dwelling in Paradise and a dwelling in Hell.

﴿They therein﴾, i.e., in the Firdaws. The feminine pronoun is used because it is a name for the Garden or for its highest level, and it is the orchard comprising all kinds of fruit. It is narrated that God built the Garden of Firdaws with a brick of gold and a brick of silver, and placed between them musk of the finest fragrance. In another narration: and a brick of pure musk, and He planted in it the best of fruits and the best of sweet basil.

﴿Abiding﴾: they will not leave it, ever. The clause is either a resumptive new sentence confirming what precedes it, or a circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah) referring to the subject or object of "yarithun", since it contains a mention of each of them. The meaning of the statement is that they will neither die nor leave it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 12:

﴿And We had certainly created man﴾ This begins an explanation of the origin of human creation and its transformation through the stages of formation and the phases of natural disposition, given in a summary manner (p-126), following an explanation of the condition of some of his fortunate individuals. The lam is the answer to an oath, and the waw is initial (ibtida'iyya); it has also been said that it is conjunctive (atifa), coordinating with what precedes it. By "man" is meant the species (al-jins), that is: by Allah, We had certainly created the species of man within the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, in a summary creation, as you have verified in (Surat al-Hajj) and elsewhere. As for his being created from extracts that were made into drops of semen after stages and phases, that is far-fetched.

﴿from an extract﴾ Sulala (extract, essence) is that which is drawn out and extracted from a thing. The pattern fu'ala is a noun for what results from an action; sometimes it is intended by the action, like khulasa (essence), and at other times it is not intended, like qulama (nail-parings) and kunasa (sweepings). Sulala belongs to the first category, since it is intended by the extracting. The "min" is initial (ibtida'iyya), connected to the creating.

The "min" in His words, ﴿of clay﴾, is explanatory (bayaniyya), connected to an omitted element that stands as a qualifier of "sulala," meaning: We created him from an extract existing as clay. It is permissible for it to be connected to "sulala" with the meaning of "that which is extracted," in which case it is initial, like the first. It has also been said: the intended "man" is Adam, peace be upon him, for he is the one who was created from a choice portion extracted from clay, and this has been verified.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 13:

﴿Then We made it﴾ i.e., the species, with regard to its individuals who are distinct from Adam, peace be upon him; or, if "the human being" is meant as Adam, peace be upon him, then "We made his offspring" with an elision of a noun (al-mudaf, the omitted governing term).

﴿a drop of sperm﴾ by Our creating him from it; or, "then We made the extract (al-sulalah) a drop." The masculine form (al-tadhkir) is by interpretation of the substance (al-jawhar), or the extracted matter (al-masul), or the water (al-ma'). ﴿in a firm place﴾, i.e., a stable receptacle, which is the womb. He expressed it by "qarar," which is a verbal noun (masdar) used for emphasis (mubalaghah).

The words of the Exalted: ﴿firmly fixed﴾ is a description of it by the attribute of that which has settled within it, like "a well-trodden path" (tariq sa'ir); or by its own firmness in itself, for it has been made firm in such a way that it is secured and guarded.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 14:

﴿Then We made the drop a clinging clot﴾. That is, coagulated blood, by turning the white drop into a red clot.

﴿Then We made the clot a lump of flesh﴾. That is, a piece of flesh in which there is no distinction or differentiation.

﴿Then We made the lump bones﴾. That is, most or all of it, by hardening it and making it a spine for the body in specific shapes and forms that wisdom requires.

﴿Then We clothed the bones﴾ (al-'izam al-ma'hudah) ﴿with flesh﴾ from the remainder of the lump, or from what We caused to grow upon them by Our power from what reaches them. That is, We clothed each bone of those bones with the flesh suitable to it, in an amount suitable to it and in a form fitting to it. The variation in the verbs is to draw attention to the differing stages of transformation, and the plural "bones" is used because they differ. It is also read in the singular in both places, relying on the collective noun, and with the singular only in the first, and with the singular only in the second.

﴿Then We produced it as another creation﴾. This refers to the form of the body, or the soul, or the faculties, by breathing into it, or to all of these together. The "then" (thumma) indicates the complete difference between the two creations. Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) used this verse as evidence that whoever usurps an egg and it hatches in his possession is liable for the egg and not for the chick, because it is "another creation."

﴿So blessed is Allah﴾, exalted is His majesty in His all-encompassing knowledge and overwhelming power. The turn to the third person in the glorious Name (al-Ism al-Jalil) serves to inspire awe and to convey wonder, and to indicate that the wondrous acts mentioned are among the judgments of divinity. It also indicates that whoever hears what has been detailed of the signs of His power, may He be exalted and mighty, or considers it, has the right to hasten to speak of it, glorifying and magnifying His affairs, exalted is He.

﴿the best of creators﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "Allah." It was also said to be a qualifier (na't) of it, on the basis that the construction (idafa) is not a verbal genitive (idafa lafziyya). It was also said to be the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), meaning: He is the best of creators in creation, that is, of those who determine by determination, the specifier (tamyiz) having been omitted, because the word "creators" indicates it, just as the permitted party (al-ma'dhun fihi) is omitted in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against…﴾, because the relative clause indicates it. That is, He is the best of creators in creation, so the excellence belongs to the creation. It was said: a parallel to this is His words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "Indeed Allah is Beautiful and loves beauty," meaning His act is beautiful. So the modified noun was omitted, the modifying noun was placed in its position, and it changed to the nominative, and so became a pronoun (istakan).

It is narrated that 'Abdullah ibn Abi Sarh used to write down revelation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When he (ﷺ) reached His words, "another creation," 'Abdullah hastened to utter it before the Prophet (ﷺ) dictated it. So he (ﷺ) said: "Write it this way; it was revealed like this." 'Abdullah doubted and said: "If Muhammad is being revealed to, then so am I." So he went to Mecca as a disbeliever, then embraced Islam on the day of the Conquest. It was also said that he died upon his disbelief.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "When this verse was revealed, 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'So blessed is Allah, the best of creators.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'It was revealed just like this, O 'Umar.'" He, may Allah be pleased with him, used to take pride in this and would say: "I agreed with my Lord in four matters: the prayer behind the Station (of Abraham), the veiling of the women, and my saying to them, 'Perhaps his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you' (and Allah revealed the verse: ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you…﴾), and the fourth: 'So blessed is Allah, the best of creators.'" Observe how this incident became a cause of 'Umar's happiness and Ibn Abi Sarh's wretchedness, as the Exalted said: ﴿He leads many astray by it and guides many by it.﴾

It is not said: humans have already spoken, from the outset, with something like the composition of the Qur'an, and that would undermine its miraculous nature. This is because what lies beyond human power is not the measure of the shortest surahs. Moreover, the miraculous nature of this noble verse is tied to what precedes it, as the particle "fa" (then) indicates, for it is a concluding parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ tadhyili) that affirms the content of what precedes it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 15:

﴿Then indeed you, after that﴾ i.e., after what has been mentioned of the marvelous matters, as is indicated by the sense of distance contained in the demonstrative (ism al-ishara), which implies the exalted rank of the one pointed to and the remoteness of his station in excellence and perfection, and his being thereby distinguished and placed in the position of sensible matters.

﴿are indeed dying﴾ i.e., surely heading toward death without any doubt, as the form of the epithet (sifa, ism al-fa'il in the sense of a nominal adjective) indicates, which denotes permanence rather than occurrence, which is what the form of the active participle (sigha al-fa'il) conveys. It has also been read: "la-ma'itun" (لَمائِتُونَ).
Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, (i.e., at the second blowing of the Trumpet) will be raised up (tub'athun) from your graves for reckoning and recompense, with reward and punishment.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 17:**

﴿And We have certainly created above you﴾ is an explanation of the creation of what their survival requires, following the explanation of their own creation; that is, We created in the direction of height, without considering its being "above" them, because that relation is only mentioned after their creation.

﴿seven paths﴾ are: the seven heavens. They were so named because some of them were stacked (ṭūriqa) upon others, like the hammering of a sandal sole (muṭārqata al-na'l), for everything that is above another like it is a ṭarīqa (path/layer). Or they were named so because they are the paths of the angels, or of the stars, in which their courses run.

﴿And We have never been unaware of the creation﴾ of that creation which is the heavens, or of all the creatures that are among its totality, or of humankind.

﴿unaware﴾ neglecting their affairs; rather, We preserve them from ceasing and disorder, and We manage their affairs until they reach the furthest point of perfection that has been decreed for them, in accordance with what wisdom requires and what the divine will has attached itself to, and so that their benefits reach what is on the earth.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 18:

Like what is indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We sent down from the sky water﴾, it is the rain, or the rivers descending from (p-128) Paradise. It has been said: they are five rivers: Sayhun, the river of India; Jayhun, the river of Balkh; the Tigris and the Euphrates, the rivers of Iraq; and the Nile, the river of Egypt. God, Exalted is He, sent them down from one of the springs of Paradise, then entrusted them to the mountains and caused them to flow in the earth, and placed in them benefits for people in the various kinds of their livelihoods. The "min" (from) is ibtida'iyyah (indicating origin) and is connected to "anzalna" (We sent down). Its being placed before the explicit object is, as has passed many times, for the sake of giving attention to what is placed first, arousing anticipation for what comes later, and turning away from the pronoun, because in the sending down what is considered is not the aspect of their being channels, but merely their being in the direction of height.

﴿with a measure﴾: with a proportion suitable for bringing about their benefits and repelling their harms, or in the amount of what We knew of their needs and their interests.

﴿then We caused it to dwell in the earth﴾: that is, We made it firm and settled in it.

﴿And indeed We are able to take it away﴾: that is, to remove it by causing it to become corrupt, or to raise it up, or to sink it deep so that its extraction becomes impossible.

﴿Surely We are able﴾, just as We were able to send it down. The indefiniteness of "dhahab" (taking away) indicates the multiplicity of its ways and an exaggeration in removing it; for this reason it was made more eloquent than His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should sink away, who would bring you flowing water?﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 19:

﴿So We brought forth for you thereby﴾ i.e., by that water, ﴿gardens of palm trees and grapevines; in them you have many fruits﴾ in the gardens, ﴿of which you partake﴾ (tafaknuhun, i.e., you enjoy them), ﴿and from them﴾ from the gardens, ﴿you eat﴾ (ta'kulun) by way of nourishment; or, you are provided for and obtain your means of livelihood, from their saying: "So-and-so eats from his trade" (ya'kulu min hirfatih). It is also permissible that the two pronouns refer to the palm trees and the grapevines, i.e., for you in their produce are kinds of fruit: fresh dates, grapes, dried dates, raisins, juice, date syrup (dibs), and other things, and food that you eat.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 20:

﴿And a tree﴾ is in the accusative case, conjoined to "gardens" (jannat). It was also read in the nominative, as a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. That is: "And among what We have produced for you by means of it is a tree." Singling it out for mention from among the trees is because it stands independently with well-known benefits. It has been said: it is the first tree that grew after the Flood. As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿that springs forth from Mount Sinai﴾, this is the Tur (mountain) of Musa, peace be upon him, between Egypt and Aylah, and it has been said [it lies] in Palestine. It is also called Tur Sinin. Either Tur is the name of the mountain and Sina' is the name of the place, and it is annexed to it, or the compound of the two is a proper name for it, like Imru' al-Qays. Its diptotic inflection (ghayr munsarif) when read with a kasra on the sin is due to definiteness and foreignness, or to femininity by interpretation as "place" (buq'ah), not because of the alif, since it is fi'al like dimas, from al-sana' with a long vowel, which means elevation, or with a short vowel, which means light, or it is assimilated to fa'lan like 'ilba' from the sin, since there is no fa'la' with the alif of femininity. This differs from Sina', for it is fay'al like kaysan, or fa'la' like sahra', since there is no fi'lal in their speech. It was also read with a kasra and a short vowel. The clause is a qualifier of "a tree," and singling it out as emerging from it, although it also emerges from all other places, is to glorify it, and because it is its original place of origin.

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿that grows with oil﴾, this is another qualifier of "a tree." The ba' is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial state (hal) of it, meaning: it grows while being accompanied by oil. It is also permissible for it to be a transitive complement, meaning: it causes it to grow, in the sense of: it contains it and produces it, since growth in reality is a quality of the tree, not of the oil. It was also read as tunbitu (causative form), and this is either from inbat in the sense of nabat, as in the verse of Zuhayr:

"I saw those in need around their houses,
their companions, until the grass grew."

Or it is by the assumption: it produces its olives accompanied by oil. It was also read in the passive, and it is like the first. Also read: tuthmiru bi-l-duhn, wa takhruju bi-l-duhn, and tanbutu bi-l-dihan.

﴿And a relish for those who eat﴾ is conjoined to "oil" and follows its grammatical case. It is the conjunction of one of two descriptions of a thing to the other, meaning: it grows with a thing that combines being oil, by which one anoints and from which lamps are fueled, and being a condiment in which bread is dipped, that is, immersed in it for the sake of eating with it. It was also read: wa-sabbagh, like dabbagh in dibgh.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 21:

﴿And indeed, in the cattle there is a lesson for you﴾ This is an explanation of the bounties overflowing upon them from the side of animals, following the explanation of the bounties reaching them from the side of water and plants. It has been made clear that these, while being in themselves a bounty from which they benefit in various ways, are a lesson which they must take heed of, drawing inferences from their conditions regarding the great power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and His abundant mercy, and that they should thank Him and not disbelieve. This was specified for animals because the locus of the lesson in them is more manifest than in plants.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We give you to drink of that which is in their bellies﴾ is a detailing of the places of lesson within them. "That which is in their bellies" is an expression that either refers to the milk, in which case "min" (from/of) is partitive (tab'idiyyah), and by "the bellies" is meant the cavity (al-jawf); or it refers to the fodder from which the milk is formed, in which case "min" is inceptive (ibtida'iyyah), and "the bellies" is in its literal sense. It has also been read with a fatha on the nun and with the ta' (nusqikum becoming tasqikum), meaning: the cattle give you to drink.

﴿And for you in them are many benefits﴾ other than what has been mentioned, such as their wool and hair, ﴿and of them you eat﴾, so you benefit from their flesh just as you benefit from what is obtained from them.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 23, verse 22:**

﴿And upon them﴾, i.e., upon the livestock (al-an'am). The carrying upon them does not require carrying upon all their kinds, but is fulfilled by carrying upon some of them, such as camels and the like. It has also been said that what is meant is camels specifically, because they are the animals that are ridden by the Arabs and are suitable to be compared with the ships (al-fulk), for they are "ships of the land" (safa'in barr). Dhu al-Rummah said:

*A ship of the land, its reins beneath my cheek...*

So the pronoun in ﴿upon them﴾ refers to camels, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And their husbands have better right to take them back﴾ (2:228), and ﴿and upon the ships you are carried﴾, i.e., on land and at sea. In combining them, the carrying upon them and upon the ships in the same expression, there is emphasis on their capacity to bear loads. This is what motivates the delaying of mention of this benefit, although it is among the benefits derived from them, until after the mention of the benefit of eating, which is connected to their very substance.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 23, verse 23:**

﴿Indeed, We sent Noah to his people.﴾ This begins an account of the previous nations' neglect and their failure to reflect and take heed of the blessings enumerated, which are restricted to the ones just mentioned, and of their failure to remember through the reminders of their messengers and the various kinds of punishment that befell them for this. It is a warning to the addressees. The placing of the story of Noah (peace be upon him) before all the other stories is evident in its wisdom. Its placement right after His words, ﴿and upon the ships you are carried﴾, carries an incomparable beauty of positioning. The *waw* is initiatory (*ibtida'iyyah*), and the *lam* is the answer to an omitted oath, and introducing the story with it shows the utmost concern for its content. That is: "By God, We indeed sent Noah," and so on. His noble lineage, the manner of his sending, and the length of his stay among them have already been explained in detail in (Surah al-A'raf) and (Surah Hud).

﴿He said﴾, showing compassion toward them and inclining them toward the truth, ﴿O my people, worship God﴾. That is: worship Him alone, as His words in Surah Hud make clear: ﴿that you worship none but God﴾. The restriction to Him was omitted to indicate that worship is exclusively that, whereas worship with associating partners is not worship at all.

His words, ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾, are a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) given to provide the reason for the worship commanded, or the reason for the command to worship. The word *ghayruhu* ("other than Him") in the nominative is an attribute of *ilah* ("god") according to its grammatical position, which is nominative, as either a subject or a predicate of a subject whose predicate is *lakum* ("for you"), or it is omitted and *lakum* is for specification and clarification. That is: "You have no god in existence or in the world other than Him, exalted is He." It is also read in the genitive according to its form.

﴿Will you not then be mindful?﴾ That is: will you not guard yourselves against His punishment, which is deserved by what you are upon of abandoning His worship? This is made clear by His words: ﴿Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day﴾ and His words: ﴿the punishment of a painful day﴾. It has been said: "Will you not fear abandoning the worship of God, who is your Lord," and so on, but this is not the right reading. It has also been said: "Will you not fear that He will remove His blessings from you," and so on, and there is much to be said about this. The interrogative particle *hamzah* is for denouncing the actual state of affairs and condemning it, and the *fa'* is for coordination with an implied element demanded by the context, that is: "Do you recognize this?", meaning the content of His words, ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾: "Will you not then guard yourselves against His punishment, because of your associating with Him in worship that does not deserve existence, were it not for God's bringing it into being, let alone deserving worship?" So the denounced matter is the failure to guard oneself while what requires it is established. Or: "Do you not take note of this, and so do not guard yourselves against Him?" Then the denounced matter is both things together, and the emphasis in that case is on quantity, while in the first it is on quality.

The chiefs (al-mala') of his people who disbelieved (﴿فَقالَ المَلأُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِن قَوْمِهِ﴾) said: "The mala' are the nobles." He described the mala' with this attribute, although all of them share it, to indicate the depth of their long-standing roots in disbelief and the firmness of their obstinacy in it. That is, they said to their common people: ﴿This is none but a human being like you﴾, meaning in species and attributes, with no distinction between you and him. They described him, peace be upon him, with this in order to exaggerate the lowering of his lofty rank and to bring him down from the station of prophethood.

﴿He wants to make himself superior over you﴾, meaning he wants to seek superiority over you and to place himself above you by claiming messengership, while being like you. They said this to anger the addressees against him, peace be upon him, and to incite them to oppose him, peace be upon him.

His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Had God willed, He would have sent down angels﴾ is an explanation of the non-existence of human messengers in absolute terms according to their corrupt assumption, after establishing his humanity, peace be upon him. That is, if God Almighty had willed to send a messenger, He would have sent messengers from among the angels. It is said "would have sent down" (la-anzala) because the sending of angels can only occur by way of descent (inzal). Thus the object of the will is the general notion of sending, understood from the answer, and not its very content, as in His saying: ﴿Had He willed, He would have guided you﴾ and its like.

﴿We have not heard of this﴾, meaning of such a speech, which is the command to worship God alone and to abandon the worship of anything other than Him. It is said that it means: of the like of Noah, peace be upon him, in claiming prophethood.

﴿among our forefathers of old﴾, meaning those who passed away before his mission, peace be upon him. They said this either because they and their forefathers were in a lengthy interval (fatrah, the period between prophets), or because of their extreme excess in denial and obstinacy and that these two were like a sorrow in error and corruption. Whichever it was, their saying this should be what came from them at the beginning of his call, peace be upon him, as the fa' in His saying: ﴿"Then the chiefs said"﴾ .. etc. indicates. It is also said that its meaning is: we have not heard of him, peace be upon him, that he is a prophet. Thus by "their forefathers of old" is meant those who passed away before them in the time of Noah, peace be upon him. Their aforementioned saying is what came from them at the final stages of his affair, peace be upon him, and it is more fitting with what follows it of the narration of his supplication, peace be upon him, and their saying.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 25:

﴿He is not﴾, i.e., what he is ﴿but a man who has madness in him﴾, i.e., insanity, or a jinn that makes them imagine it; and for this reason he says what he says.

﴿So wait over him﴾, i.e., bear with him, be patient with him, and wait.

﴿for a time﴾, perhaps he will recover from what is in him. (p-131) This is then to be understood in light of the wide range of their conditions in obstinacy and stubbornness, and their turning away from what they described him, peace be upon him, as having of humanity, and their desire to attribute to him, peace be upon him, a description other than what you see, while they know that he, peace be upon him, is the most sound-minded of people in intellect and the most weighty of people in speech. And according to the first reading, [it is] on the contradiction of their corrupt statements. May Allah fight them; how are they deluded?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 26:

﴿Said﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new sentence) built upon a question that arises from the narration of the words of the disbelievers. It is as if it were said: "What did he (peace be upon him) say after hearing from them these falsehoods?" So it is answered: He said, when he saw that they had persisted in disbelief and denial, and had gone on in error and misguidance, until he despaired of their faith entirely, and God had revealed to him that none of your people will believe except those who have already believed: ﴿My Lord, help me﴾ by destroying them utterly. This is a summary narration of his (peace be upon him) words: ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth any of the disbelievers a dweller [of the land]﴾, and so on.

﴿Because they denied me﴾ meaning: because of their denial of me, or it is a substitute (badal) for their denial.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 27:

﴿So We revealed to him﴾ at that time: ﴿"Build the ship under Our eyes and by Our revelation"﴾. "An" (that) is explanatory (mufassirah), clarifying what in the revelation (wahy) carries the sense of speech (qawl). ﴿Under Our eyes﴾ means accompanied by Our protection and Our watchfulness, as if with him, peace be upon him, from Him, the Mighty and Exalted, there were guardians and protectors who watch over him with their eyes, from transgression or from error in the craftsmanship.

﴿And Our revelation﴾: that is, Our command and Our instruction on how to make it.

The fa' (so) in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So when Our command comes﴾ is for ordering the content of what follows upon the completion of the building of the ship. By "the command" is meant the punishment, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿There is no protector today from the command of God﴾ (Qur'an 11:43), not the command to board, as has been said. Its coming signifies the culmination of its approach or the beginning of its appearance; that is, when Our punishment comes right after the completion of the ship. His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and the oven boils over﴾ are an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to the coming of the command. It is related that it was said to him, peace be upon him: "When water boils over from the oven, board, you and those with you." The oven was that of Adam, peace be upon him, which passed to Noah, peace be upon him. When water gushed from it, his wife informed him, and they boarded. There is disagreement about its location. It is said that it was in the mosque of Kufa, that is, in its place on the right of one entering through the Kindah gate today. It is also said that it was in the spring of Warda in Syria. Its details have already been discussed in the commentary on (Surat Hud), peace be upon him.

﴿Then load into it﴾: that is, enter into it. It is said: salaka fihi, meaning he entered it, and salakahu fihi meaning he caused him to enter it. From this is His words, Exalted is He: ﴿What has brought you into Saqar?﴾ (Qur'an 74:42).

﴿From every﴾: that is, from every nation ﴿two pairs﴾: that is, two single ones paired together, as His words, Exalted is He, indicate: ﴿two﴾ (Qur'an 11:40), which is explicit about two individuals and not two groups or two classes. It is also read with the genitive construction, on the basis that the object is "two", that is, from every nation of Mine, two pairs, namely the nation of the male and the nation of the female, like camels and she-camels, horses and mares. This is explicit that the command preceded his building of the ship. In Surat Hud: ﴿until when Our command came and the oven boiled over, We said: load into it two of every pair﴾ (Qur'an 11:40). The proper reading is either that it is a report of another, immediate command given at the boiling of the oven, to which the conditional command was attached, out of concern for the matter commanded; or that this is the same earlier command. But since the conditional command, before the condition is realized, has no binding force regarding the commanded act, it is treated as though it occurred only when the condition was realized, and so it is reported in the form of an immediate command. This has already been discussed in the commentary on His words: (p-132) Exalted is He: ﴿And when We said to the angels: prostrate to Adam﴾ (Qur'an 2:34).

﴿And your family﴾ is in the accusative, governed by a verb coordinated with "fa-usluk", not coordinated with "two pairs" or "two" in either reading, because that would lead to a disruption of meaning. That is: and load your family. By it is meant his wife and sons. The delay in mentioning their entry, relative to what was mentioned about the entry of the pairs, is because he is in the process of striving with what he was commanded regarding the entry, for he needs to undertake work himself, and indeed needs help from his family and followers. As for them, they enter it by their own choice afterward. Also, because in the latter there is a kind of detail by mentioning the exception and other things, so placing it first would disrupt the harmony of the parts of the noble composition.

﴿Except him against whom the word has already preceded among them﴾: that is, the word concerning the destruction of the disbelievers. The preposition "ʿala" is used because the preceding word is harmful, just as the lam is used in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed those for whom the best has preceded from Us﴾ (Qur'an 21:101), because it is beneficial.

﴿And do not address Me concerning those who did wrong﴾ by asking for their deliverance ﴿Indeed they are to be drowned﴾: this is a justification for the prohibition, or for what it indicates of the non-acceptance of the supplication; that is, they are decreed to be drowned without doubt because of their wrongdoing through polytheism and other sins. Whoever is in such a state is not interceded for, nor is intercession granted on his behalf.

How could it not be so, when he was commanded to give thanks for being saved from them by their destruction, through His saying: ﴿So when you and those who are with you have settled into the ship﴾, that is, of your family and followers, ﴿then say: "All praise is for God, who has saved us from the wrongdoing people."﴾ This is in the manner of His saying: ﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off. And all praise is for God, Lord of the worlds.﴾

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 29:

﴿And say: "My Lord, cause me to disembark at a blessed place of disembarkation"﴾ — in the ship or out of it — ﴿a blessed place of disembarkation﴾; that is: a disembarking (inzal), or a place of disembarkation that brings about abundant good. It is also read "munzalan" (مُنْزَلًا), meaning a place of descent (mawdi' nuzul).

﴿And You are the best of those who bring to land﴾. He (peace be upon him) was commanded to preface his supplication with praise of Him, the Mighty and Majestic, that matches it, as a means of seeking a response. His being singled out for the command, although all of them shared in the settling and the deliverance, serves to show his favour (peace be upon him) and to indicate that in his supplication and praise there is a sufficiency (mandiha) beyond anything else.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 23, verse 30:**

﴿Indeed, in that﴾, that which was mentioned of what was done to him (peace be upon him) and to his people, ﴿are signs﴾, magnificent ones, by which those of insight are guided and by which those who take lessons are admonished.

﴿And indeed, We were ever sending trials﴾. "Inna" is the lightened form (mukhaffafah) of "anna", and the "lam" is the distinguishing lam (lam al-farqiyah) that separates it from the negating "in". The pronoun of the matter (ḍamir al-sha'n) is omitted. That is: "Indeed the matter is that We were ever striking the people of Noah with a great affliction and severe punishment, and testing Our servants by these signs, so that We might see who takes heed and remembers," like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly left it as a sign, so is there anyone who will take heed?﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 31:

﴿Then We produced after them﴾ i.e., after their destruction, ﴿another generation﴾. They were the people of ʿĀd, as related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, and it is the view of most exegetes (mufassirūn), and it is the most suitable, in light of the established practice in the other noble surahs of mentioning their story right after the story of the people of Noah. It was also said: they were Thamūd.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 32:

﴿So We sent among them﴾ They made it a place for the sending (ilsal), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus We sent you to a nation﴾, and similar, which has no limit, as in the like of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people﴾, to make known from the outset that the one who was sent to them did not come to them from outside their place, but rather grew up among them, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿a messenger from among them﴾, that is, from their own number by lineage, for both of them, peace be upon them, were from among them.

And "an" (that) in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Worship Allah﴾ is explanatory (mufassirah) for "We sent," because it includes the meaning of saying, that is: We said to them through the tongue of the Messenger, "Worship Allah, exalted is He." And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾ is a reason (ta'lil) for the worship commanded, or for the command to it, or for the obligation of compliance with it.

﴿Will you not then fear (God)?﴾ That is: His punishment, which is called for by what you are upon of polytheism (shirk) and sins. The discussion regarding the conjunction (i'tiraf) is like what passed in the story of Noah, peace be upon him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 33:

﴿And the chiefs of his people said﴾ is a narration of their false saying, following the narration of the true saying spoken by the narration of the sending of the Messenger, by way of conjunction (ʿaṭf), on the understanding that the intent is the narration of their denial of him, peace be upon him, in general terms, not the narration of what passed between him, peace be upon him, and them of dialogue and debate in detail, such that it would be narrated by way of resumption (istiʾnaf) built upon a question, as is indicated by what will come of the narration of the rest of the nations. That is: and the nobles of his people said.

﴿Who disbelieved﴾ is in the place of the nominative (rafʿ), as an attribute (ṣifah) of the chiefs (al-malaʾ). They were described with this as a reproach of them and as an alert to their excess in disbelief. Its placement after "of his people" is because of the conjunction of His statement, exalted is He, ﴿and denied the meeting of the Hereafter﴾ and what is conjoined to it, to the first relative clause (ṣilah). That is: they denied the meeting with what is in it of reckoning, reward and punishment, or their return to the second life by resurrection.

﴿And We had given them luxury﴾, meaning, We had pampered them ﴿in the life of this world﴾ with abundance of wealth and children. That is: they said to their successors, misleading them, ﴿This is only a human being like you﴾, that is, in attributes and conditions. The choice of "like you" over "like us" is for the sake of intensifying the belittling of his matter, peace be upon him, and weakening it.

﴿He eats of what you eat from, and drinks of what you drink﴾ is an affirmation of the likeness. "Mā" is a descriptive (khabariyyah) relative pronoun, and the returning pronoun to the second is an omitted accusative object, or a genitive that has been omitted together with its preposition, because of what precedes it indicating it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 34:

﴿And if you obey a human being like yourselves﴾, i.e., in the conditions and attributes mentioned, that is, if you comply with his commands, ﴿then indeed you would be, at that point﴾, i.e., on the supposition of following him, ﴿losers﴾, losing your intellects and being defrauded in your opinions, in that you have humbled yourselves. Consider how they regarded following the true Messenger, who conveys them to the happiness of both abodes, as a loss, while worshipping idols, beyond which there is no loss, [as a gain]. May God fight them: how are they deluded! And "idha" (then/in that case) occurs between the subject of "inna" (indeed) and its predicate, to emphasize the content of the conditional clause, and the clause is the answer to an omitted oath preceding the conditional "in" (if) introduced by the connecting lam (al-lam al-muwatti'ah), i.e., "By God, if you obey a human being like yourselves, then indeed you would be losers."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 35:

﴿Does he promise you﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), brought to confirm what precedes it, namely their being rebuked for following him (peace be upon him) by denying the occurrence of what would call them to faith in him, and by deeming it remote.

﴿That when you die﴾ is read with a kasra on the mim, from māta yamūtu (to die). It is also read with a damma on the mim, from mātа yamūtu (to die), [as variant reading].

﴿and you have become dust and bones﴾, bones that are decayed and stripped of flesh and sinews; that is, some of your parts were flesh and the like, and they became dust, and some of them were bones. The mention of dust first is due to its being the most remarkable in terms of remoteness (istib'ad) and its transformation from the visible parts. Or, your predecessors were pure dust and your successors were bones.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed you﴾ is an emphatic restatement of the first (inna) because of the long separation between it and its predicate, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿will be brought forth﴾, that is, from the graves alive as you were. It has been said: ﴿That you will be brought forth﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), and "when you die" is its predicate, meaning: your bringing forth when you die; then he informed about the whole clause concerning "that you". It has also been said: ﴿that you will be brought forth﴾ is raised by a verb which is the apodosis of the conditional, as if it were said: when you die, your bringing forth occurs; then the conditional clause was made a predicate of "that you". What the eloquence of the noble composition requires is the first view. It is also read: "Does he promise you, when you have died," etc.

﴿Hayhata hayhata﴾ is a repetition for emphasis of distance, meaning: the distance of occurrence or of truth, ﴿for what you are promised﴾. It has been said that the lam (in ﴿limā﴾) is for specifying what is deemed remote, as in "hayta laka" (the lam indicating the addressee), as if when they uttered the word of remoteness, it was said: "Why this remoteness?" So it was said: "for what you are promised." It has also been said that hayhata means distance, and it is a mubtada' (subject) whose khabar (predicate) is ﴿limā tū'adūn﴾ (for what you are promised).

It was read with a fatha and with tanwin, for indefiniteness (hayhatan, hayhatan), and with a damma with tanwin, on the basis that it is the plural of hayha (hayhatun) [pl. hayhāt]; and without tanwin, imitating qabl (as in qabluʾ, a form of an adverb of time). It was also read with a kasra on both the options, and with a sukun, following the pronunciation at pause, with the ta' changed to ha'.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 37:

﴿In hiya illa hayatuna al-dunya﴾ Its original form is: in al-hayatu illa hayatuna, and the pronoun was placed in the position of the first (noun) to indicate the second upon it, out of caution against repetition and in order to make it sufficient without explicit statement, as in: "She is the soul (nafs), it bears what it is made to bear," and "She is the Arabs (al-'Arab), they say what they wish." Since the pronoun carries the meaning of life, which denotes the genus, the negating "in" (in al-nafiya) holds the position of the negating "la" (la al-nafiya) for the genus. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Namutu wa nahya﴾ ("We die and we live") is a sentence explaining what they claimed, namely that life is the life of this world; that is, some of us die and some are born, until the era passes away.

﴿Wa ma nahnu bi-mab'uthin﴾ ("And we shall not be resurrected") after death.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 38:

﴿In huwa﴾ i.e., ma huwa ﴿illa rajulun iftara 'ala Allahi kadhiban﴾ in what he claims of being sent [as a messenger] and in what he promises us, that God will resurrect us.

﴿Wa ma nahnu lahu bi-mu'minin﴾ we are not believers in him, i.e., we do not confirm what he says.

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 23, verse 39:

﴿He said﴾: that is, Hud (peace be upon him), when he despaired of their believing after having pursued every method in calling them, humbly beseeching Allah, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿My Lord, help me﴾ against them, and avenge me upon them.

﴿Because they denied me﴾: that is, because of their denying me and their persistence in it.

﴿He said﴾ — the Most High said, in response to his supplication and as a promise of acceptance.

﴿After a little while﴾ — i.e., after a short time. The particle "mā" (ما) is here a superfluous addition (mazīdah) between the preposition and the noun it governs, to emphasise the meaning of paucity, just as it is added in His words, ﴿So by a mercy from Allah...﴾. Alternatively, it is an indefinite noun described by an adjective, meaning: after a small thing, i.e., after a little time.

﴿They will surely become regretful﴾ — for what they had done of denial, and that will be at the time they witness the punishment.

(p-135) ﴿So the Cry seized them﴾. Perhaps when the barren wind struck them, they were also struck within it by a terrible cry. It is related that Shaddad ibn 'Ad, when he had completed the building of Iram, set out for it with his people. When he drew near it, God sent upon them a cry from heaven, and they perished. It is also said that the Cry is the very punishment and death itself, and it is said that it is a punishment that uproots. One of them said:

The age cried out against the family of Barmak with a cry;
they fell prostrate on their chins from its severity.

﴿in truth﴾ relates to the seizing: that is, by a matter that is established and that none can repel, or by justice from God Most High, or by a true promise.

﴿And We made them debris﴾: that is, like the debris of a torrent, which is what the flood carries along.

﴿So away with the wrongdoing people﴾: this is either a statement or a supplication. "Bu'dan" (بُعْدًا) is among the verbal nouns whose verb is rarely used. The meaning is: they went far away, that is, they perished. The lam (اللَّامُ) is to specify who is meant by "away." The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to indicate the cause.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 42:

﴿Then We brought into being, after them,﴾ that is, after their destruction, ﴿other generations.﴾ They were the people of Salih, Lut, and Shu'ayb, peace be upon them, and others besides them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 43:

﴿No nation can hasten its term﴾. That is: no nation of the destroyed peoples can go ahead of the time appointed for their destruction; that is, no nation is destroyed before its appointed term comes.

﴿Nor can they delay it by an hour﴾. That term does not get postponed by even an hour.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 44:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "We brought into being" (anshaʾnā), but not in the sense that their sending was delayed relative to the bringing into being of all the generations mentioned together; rather, in the sense that the sending of each messenger was subsequent to the bringing into being of a particular generation specific to that messenger. It is as if it were said: Then We brought into being after them other generations, to each generation of whom We sent a messenger specific to it. The separation between the two conjoined clauses by the parenthetical sentence, which states that the nations did not precede their appointed term of destruction, is for the sake of hastening to the explanation of their destruction in a general manner.

﴿Tatra⁠ (tatrā)﴾ means: consecutively, one after another, from the root witr, which is the single (fard). The tāʾ is a substitution for a wāw, as in tūlij and yattaqū, and the alif is for the feminine, in consideration of the messengers being a group. It has also been read with tanwīn, as a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the sense of the active participle, occurring as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Every time there came to a nation its messenger, they denied him﴾ is a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf) explaining the coming of each messenger to his nation and what proceeded from them at the conveying of the message. By "coming" is meant either conveying (tablīgh), or the literal coming, to indicate that they denied him at the first encounter. The attribution of the messenger to the nation, together with the attribution of all of them earlier to the plural of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓama), is to establish that each messenger came to his own particular nation, not that all of them came to all the nations; and it conveys the completeness of their vileness and error, in that each nation denied its specific messenger. It has also been said: because sending is fitting for the one sent, and coming is fitting for the one sent to them.

﴿So We caused them to follow one another [in destruction]﴾, in destruction, just as some of them followed others in engaging in its causes, which are disbelief, denial, and all other sins.

﴿And We made them into tales﴾: nothing of them remained except narratives from which those who take heed might learn. It is either a collective noun (ism jamʿ) for ḥadīth, or the plural of uḥdūthah, which is what is spoken of for diversion, like aʿājīb, the plural of uʿjūbah, which is what one marvels at. That is: We made them into tales spoken of for diversion and wonder.

﴿So away with a people who do not believe﴾: here He restricted their description to non-belief, just as He restricted the narration of their denial to a general statement. As for the earlier generations, where what preceded of extremism and transgression of bounds in disbelief and aggression was reported about them, they were described as wrongdoers (ẓulm).

(p-136)

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 23, verse 45:**

﴿Then We sent Musa and his brother Harun with Our signs﴾: these are the nine signs: the hand, the staff, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the diminishing of the fruits, and the plague. There is no room to count the splitting of the sea among them, since the intended meaning is the signs that they denied and against which they were arrogant.

﴿And a manifest authority﴾: that is, a clear proof that binds the adversary. It is either the staff, which is singled out for mention although it is included among the signs, because it is the mother of his signs, peace be upon him, and the first of them. Many miracles (mu'jizat) are connected to it, such as its turning into a serpent and its swallowing what the magicians had falsified, as explained in the tafsir (exegesis) of (Surah Ta-Ha). As for mentioning the splitting of the sea, the bursting of springs from the rock by its striking, its guarding, its becoming a candle and a green fruit-bearing tree, a bucket and a rope, and other things that appeared through it before and after, outside the presence of Pharaoh and his people, this is not suitable to the requirement of the context. As for the signs themselves, such as the saying "To the lordly king and the son of the valiant one... etc.," he expressed them by that in the manner of conjunction (ʿatf), to draw attention to their being gathered under two sublime headings, and to treat the difference between them as if it were an essential difference.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 46:

﴿To Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾, that is, the nobles of his people. They were singled out for mention because the sending of the Children of Israel was entrusted to their opinions, not to the opinions of their followers.

﴿But they waxed proud﴾, refusing to submit and rebelling, ﴿and they were a haughty people﴾, arrogant and insolent.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 47:

﴿So they said﴾ is conjoined (ʿatf) to "they were arrogant" (istakbarū), and what lies between them is an interjected clause (iʿtirāḍ) that confirms their arrogance, i.e., they were a people whose habit was arrogance and rebelliousness. That is, they said among themselves, by way of counsel: ﴿Shall we believe in two mortals like ourselves?﴾ The word "mortals" (basharayn) is dual because bashar may be used for the singular, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿a perfect human (basharan sawiyyan)﴾, just as it may be used for the plural, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿If you see any human (min al-bashar aḥadan)﴾. The word "like" (mithl) is not made dual, in view of its being in the status of a verbal noun (maṣdar). These narratives, as we see, indicate that the basis of the doubts of those who deny prophethood is measuring the condition of the prophets by their own conditions, on the basis of their ignorance of the details of the affairs of human reality and of the variance of the ranks of its individuals in the levels of perfection and the abysses of deficiency. So some of them are at the highest of the highest (ʿilliyyūn), namely those specially endowed with pure souls, supported by holy power, who, because of the purity of their essences, are connected to both the spiritual and the corporeal worlds; they receive from one side and impart to the other, and their attachment to the interests of creatures does not hinder them from devotion to the presence of the Truth. And some of them are at the lowest of the low, like those ignorant ones who are like cattle, nay, they are further astray in the way.

﴿And their people﴾, meaning the Children of Israel, ﴿are our servants﴾, i.e., serving and submissive to us as slaves. It seems they intended by this to disparage the two of them, peace be upon them, and to lower their exalted rank from the office of messengership by another aspect apart from humanity. The lām in "lanā" is connected to "ʿābidūn" and was placed before it for the sake of the rhyme (fawāṣil). The clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "nu'minu," confirming the denial of belief in them, based on their corrupt assumption founded on analogizing religious leadership to worldly leaderships, which revolve around precedence in obtaining base enjoyments of wealth and rank, like the practice of Quraysh when they said: ﴿Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾, and ﴿They said: Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two towns?﴾, and their ignorance that the criterion for selection to messengership is precedence in acquiring the lofty qualities mentioned and securing the exalted attributes, both innately and by acquisition.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 48:

﴿So they denied them﴾, i.e., they persisted in denying the two of them, insisted upon it, and acted with great arrogance. ﴿So they were among the destroyed﴾ by drowning in the sea of Qulzum.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 49:**

﴿And We certainly gave﴾, that is, after Their destruction and the deliverance of the Children of Israel from their dominion, ﴿Moses the Book﴾, that is, the Torah. Since his giving it to his people, peace be upon him, was for guiding his people to the truth, as is the case with the divine Books, they were treated as though they had been given it. Hence it was said: ﴿so that they may be guided﴾, that is, to the path of truth by acting upon what it contains of laws and rulings. It was also said: the intended meaning is "We gave [it to] the people of Moses," so the genitive construction (mudaf) was omitted and the genitive complement (mudaf ilayhi) was put in its place, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in fear of Pharaoh and their chiefs...﴾, that is, "of the family of Pharaoh and their chiefs." There is no way to return the pronoun to Pharaoh and his people, because it is evident that the Torah was revealed only after their drowning, when they had drowned the Children of Israel. As for citing for this the verse ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book after We had destroyed the earlier generations﴾, it is something that cannot be accepted, since it is necessarily not the case that "the earlier generations" refers to the people of Pharaoh, but rather, specifically, the nations destroyed before them, such as the people of Noah, the people of Hud, the people of Salih, and the people of Lot, as will come in (Surat al-Qasas).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 50:**

﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾. And what a sign it was, indicating the great power of Ours in his being born of her without the touch of a human being. The "sign" is then one matter attributed to both of them. Or: We made the son of Mary a sign by his speaking in the cradle, whereby numerous miracles appeared from him, and his mother a sign in that she bore him without touch; the first was omitted because the second indicates it. The expressing of them both by the two designations mentioned, namely his, upon him be peace, being her son and her being his mother, peace be upon him, is to signal from the outset the aspect of their both being a sign. For his, upon him be peace, being attributed to her, despite the fact that attribution to fathers is customary, indicates that he had no father, meaning: We made the son of Mary alone, without his having a father, and his mother who bore him alone, without the participation of a father, a sign. His, upon him be peace, being mentioned first is because of his primacy in what has been mentioned of being a sign, just as the mention of his mother first in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾ is because of her primacy in what is attributed to her of chastity and the breathing (of the spirit).

﴿And We sheltered them on a high ground﴾, that is, on elevated land. It has been said: it is Ilya, the land of Bayt al-Maqdis, for it is elevated, and it is the navel of the earth and the closest land to the sky by eighteen miles, according to what is related from Ka'b. And it has been said: Damascus and its Ghouta; and it has been said: Palestine and Ramla; and it has been said: Egypt, for its villages are on high ground. It was read with the ra' vowelled with kasra and with damma, and "ribawah" with kasra and damma.

﴿Possessing stability﴾: a settled place of level, smooth land on which its inhabitants settle. It has been said: possessing fruits and crops, for which its inhabitants settle there. ﴿And a flowing spring﴾: that is, and water, flowing, apparent. It is fa'il from ma'ana the water, when it flowed; its root meaning is distance in walking, or it is from al-ma'un, which is benefit, because it is beneficial; or it is maf'ul from 'anahu, when he perceived it with the eye, for due to its prominence it is perceived by the eyes. Its water was described thus to signal that it combines the varieties of benefits: drinking, watering what is watered of animals and plants without hardship, and recreation by its well-arranged sight.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 51:

﴿O messengers, eat of the good things⟩ is a narration of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a general form, referring to what was addressed to every messenger in his time. It is placed right after the narration of the sheltering of 'Isa (peace be upon him) and his mother on the high ground, to signal that the provision of the means of enjoyment was not among his special features (peace be upon him), but rather the permission of good things is an ancient law which all the messengers (peace be upon them) followed and enjoined. That is: We said to every messenger, "Eat of the good things and do righteous deeds." So the many commands addressed to the messengers were expressed in the plural form when narrated, in summary, for brevity. In it there is a clear indication of the falsity of the position of the monks (al-rahabina), who reject good things. It has also been said: it is a narration of what was said to 'Isa (peace be upon him) and his mother when they were sheltered on the high ground, so that they might follow the messengers in partaking of what they had been provided. It has also been said: it is an address and a direct speech to him, with the plural used for honor. From al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi, and al-Kalbi, may Allah have mercy on them all: it is an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) alone, in accordance with the Arab habit of addressing a single person with the plural form. In it there is a demonstration of his excellence and that he stands in place of all of them in possessing their perfections. "The good things" (al-tayyibat) are what is agreeable and pleasurable among permissible foods and fruits, as indicated by the context of the noble verse; so the command is for enjoyment.

﴿And act righteously⟩ i.e., a righteous deed, for that is what is intended from you and beneficial in the sight of your Lord.

﴿Indeed I am, of what you do⟩ of outward and inward deeds, ﴿All-Knowing⟩; I will recompense you for it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 52:

﴿And indeed, this﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) included within what the Messengers, upon them be peace, were addressed with in the aforementioned manner. It is brought to explain that the religion of Islam and monotheism (tawhid) is something all the Messengers, upon them be peace, and all the nations were commanded with. It is pointed to with "this" only to draw attention to the complete clarity of its matter in soundness and rectitude, and to its being organized, by reason of that, within the course of matters that are observed.

﴿Your community﴾, i.e., your religion and your law, O Messengers, ﴿is one community﴾, i.e., one religion and one law, unified in the fundamentals of the laws, which do not change with the change of eras. It has also been said: "this" refers to the nations that believed in the Messengers, and the meaning is: this, your congregation, is one congregation, agreed upon faith and monotheism in worship.

﴿And I am your Lord﴾ without there being any partner for Me in lordship. The pronoun of address in it, and in the words of the Exalted: ﴿so fear Me﴾, i.e., by splitting the staff and opposing, by neglecting what is required of what was mentioned of the exclusivity of lordship to Me, for the Messengers and the nations alike. The command regarding the Messengers is for stirring up and inspiring, and regarding the nations it is for warning and obligation. The "fa" (so) is for the ordering of the command, or the obligation of complying with it, upon what precedes it of the exclusivity of lordship to the Exalted and the unity of the community, for each of these necessarily requires taqwa (God-consciousness).

It was also read: "wa-anna hadhihi" with the hamza opened, by omitting the lam, i.e., "and because this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so fear Me," meaning: if you fear, then fear Me, as has passed in the words of the Exalted: ﴿and Me, so fear Me﴾. It has also been said: it is in coordination with "ma" (what), i.e., "I know that your community is a community," etc. It has also been said: it is by omitting a verb governing it, i.e., "and know that this is your community," etc.

It was also read: "wa-in hadhihi" as a lightened form of "inna" (indeed).

(p-139) ﴿So they cut their affair into pieces among themselves﴾: a narration of what appeared from the nations of the Messengers after them, of opposing the command and splitting the staff (of unity). The pronoun refers to what is indicated by "the community" (ummah) of their lords, first according to both interpretations (of tafsir). The fa' (then) denotes the sequence of their disobedience to the command, to add to the censure of their state; that is: they cut the matter of their religion into pieces, although it is one, and made it scattered fragments and differing religions.

﴿between them into scriptures﴾: that is, pieces, the plural of zubur, in the sense of sects (firqah). It is conveyed by the reading "zubaran" with a fatha on the ba', the plural of zabrah, and it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "amrahum", or from the waw of "taqatta'u", or a second object (maf'ul thani) of it, since it implicitly contains the meaning of "ja'alu" (made) and "qabila" (took), so that it is a second object, or a circumstantial clause from "amrahum" with the deletion of a modifier, that is: like scriptures (zubur). It was also read with the ba' lightened, like rusl for rusul.

﴿every faction, with what they have, rejoicing﴾: of those factions that split into parties, ﴿with what they have﴾ of the religion which they have chosen, ﴿rejoicing﴾: pleased with it, believing that it is the truth.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 54:

﴿So leave them in their bewilderment for a time.﴾ The state they are in of ignorance is likened to water that covers the stature (qamah), because they are submerged in it, playing with it. It is also read as "ghamaratihim" (their overwhelming waves/depths), and the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The fa' (fa, the "so" particle) indicates that the command to leave them is ordered upon what precedes it, namely their being exultant with what they have; for their absorption in what they are in and their persistence in it are indications that their hearts have been sealed, i.e., leave them in their state.

﴿until a time﴾ is the time of their being killed, or their dying in disbelief, or their punishment. So it is a warning to them of punishment in this world and the Hereafter, a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and a prohibition to him against hastening their punishment and against impatience at its delay. In the indefiniteness (tankir) and the vagueness (ibham) there is what is not hidden of awesome intimidation (tahwil).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 55:

﴿Do they reckon that by what We extend to them﴾ — that is, We give them it and make it an extension (madad) for them. Here "ma" is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿of wealth and children﴾ is an explanation (bayan) of it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 56:

The placing of wealth before children, even though they are more dear than it, has already had its reason explained in (Surat al-Kahf). It is not the predicate of inna (inna, "indeed"). Rather, the predicate is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿We hasten to them with good things﴾, with the returning pronoun to the subject omitted, meaning: Do they reckon that what We extend to them of wealth and children, We hasten for them therein toward that in which is their good and their honor? Here the hamzah (hamzah, the interrogative particle) is for denying what has occurred and deeming it abhorrent.

And His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Nay, they do not perceive﴾ is a conjunction with an implied clause that the speech extends over, meaning: No, We do not do that; rather they do not perceive anything at all, like the beasts that have no discernment and no awareness, so that they would reflect and realize that this extension is a gradual leading-on for them and a drawing them on to an increase in sin, while they think it is a hastening for them in good things. It has been read: "yumidduhum" (yumiddu-hum, "He extends them") in the third person, and likewise "yusari'u" (yusari'u, "He hastens") and "yusri'u" (yusri'u, "He hastens") and it is possible that in both there is a pronoun referring to the one who extends with it. It has also been read: "yusari'u" in the passive voice (mabni li-l-maf'ul, passive form).

Verse 57 of Surah 23 (al-Mu'minun): ﴿Indeed, those who are fearful out of awe of their Lord﴾ is a resumed statement (isti'naf) brought to explain who it is that hastens toward good deeds, following the despair of the disbelievers regarding them and the nullification of their false presumption. That is: they are wary out of fear of His punishment.
(p-140) ﴿Those who believe in the signs of their Lord﴾, both those set up (in creation) and those sent down (in revelation), ﴿believe﴾ by affirming what they signify.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 59:

﴿And those who do not associate anything with their Lord﴾ — neither overt association (shirk jali) nor hidden association (shirk khafi). For this reason it is mentioned after belief in the signs (al-ayat). The mention of the title "Lord" (al-rububiyya) in the three positions is to indicate that it is the reason (illiyya) for the apprehensive fear (al-ishfaq), the belief (al-iman), and the absence of association (adam al-ishrak).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 60:
