﴿Those who give what they give﴾ i.e., they give what they have given of charities (sadaqat). It has also been read: "ya'tūna mā ātaw" (they do what they have done), i.e., they perform what they have done of acts of obedience (ta'at). In either case, the past tense form in the second relative clause serves to indicate certainty (tahaqquq), just as the present tense form in the first serves to indicate continuity (istimrar).

﴿And their hearts are fearful﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the subject of "yu'tūn" or "ya'tūn", i.e., they give what they have given, or they perform the acts of worship that they have performed, while the circumstance is that their hearts are frightened, in the utmost degree of fear.

﴿That they are returning to their Lord﴾ i.e., [the fear is] that their return to Him, mighty and majestic, is such that the cause of their fear is that this (their deeds) might not be accepted from them, and that it might not occur in the proper manner, so that they would be held accountable for it at that time, not merely that they return to Him, exalted is He. It has been said: "because their place of return is to Him, exalted is He." The four relative pronouns refer to one single group characterized by what is mentioned within the scope of their relative clauses of the four attributes, not to separate groups each characterized by one of the attributes mentioned; as if it were said: "Those who are apprehensive of the fear of their Lord, and who believe in the signs of their Lord..." etc. The relative pronoun was repeated only to signal that each of those attributes is independently a distinguished virtue in its own right, and to treat the independence of each as the independence of the thing described by them.

﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ is a demonstrative referring to them, in view of their being characterized by these qualities. The distance implied in it indicates the elevated rank they hold in excellence. That is, "those who are described by the noble qualities detailed above, exclusively and not others."

﴿يُسارِعُونَ في الخَيْراتِ﴾ means they hasten to attain the good things, among which are the goods of this world promised for righteous deeds, as in His saying, ﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the excellent reward of the Hereafter﴾, and His saying, ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾. Thus what was denied of their opposites is affirmed for them, except that the wording was changed. He did not say, "We hasten to them with good things," but rather attributed the hastening to them, indicating their full worthiness to attain the good things through the excellence of their deeds. The choice of the word "fi" (in) over "ila" (to) signals that they are immersed in various kinds of good things, and that they are not merely turning towards them from outside, but are moving through them in haste, as in His saying, ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a garden﴾, and so on.

﴿وَهم لَها سابِقُونَ﴾ means they outstrip others to them. The lam (ل) strengthens the government of the verb, as in His saying, ﴿They are doing deeds for it﴾, meaning they attain them before the Hereafter, since they are hastened to them in this world. It was also said that the intended meaning of "the good things" is acts of obedience, and the meaning is: they desire acts of obedience and worship with the greatest desire, and for their sake they are those who precede in performing them, or for their sake they outstrip people. The first interpretation is the preferable one. (p-141)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 62:

﴿And We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity.﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (*jumla musta'nifa*, a sentence that begins a new point while connecting to what precedes it), brought to encourage what the foregoing were described as doing: performing acts of obedience that lead to attaining good things. It does so by showing how easy these acts are and that they do not exceed the limit of one's capacity and strength. That is, Our custom is established that We do not burden any soul among souls except with what is within its capacity. The intended meaning is the continuation of the negation (*istimrar al-nafy*, the negation being sustained) through the help of the context, not the negation of continuance (*nafy al-istimrar*), as has been mentioned repeatedly. Alternatively, the verse is for granting leniency (*al-tarkhis*) regarding what falls short of the level of the deeds of those righteous people. It shows that He, exalted is He, does not burden His servants except with what is within their capacity. So if they do not reach the ranks of the foremost (*al-sabiqun*) in performing acts of obedience, there is no blame on them after they have spent their utmost effort and exhausted their capacity.

Muqatil said: Whoever is unable to stand should pray seated, and whoever is unable to sit should pray by gesturing (*fa-yumi ima'an*).

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And with Us is a Book﴾ etc. is a continuation of what precedes it, explaining the state of the actions they were charged with and the rulings concerning them that follow from them: reckoning, reward and punishment. By "the Book" is meant the records of deeds that they will read at the reckoning, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It speaks with the truth﴾, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is Our Record; it speaks against you with the truth. Indeed, We were having copied what you used to do.﴾ That is: with Us is a Book in which the deeds of every person are recorded as they are, or the deeds of the foremost and the moderate (*al-muqtasidun*) all together, not that the deeds of the first were recorded and the deeds of the later were neglected. In this there is also a cutting off of their excuse.

As for His saying "bi-al-haqq" (with the truth): it is connected (*muta'allaq*, governed as a complement) to *yanti'u* (it speaks). That is, it makes manifest the truth that corresponds to reality as it is, in essence and attribute, and clarifies it to the one who looks, just as speech clarifies it, and makes it manifest to the hearer. Thereby the great and the minute details of their deeds become apparent there, and He arranges upon them the recompense: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ is an explanation of His grace and justice in recompense, following the explanation of His kindness in imposing obligations and recording deeds. That is: they will not be wronged in the recompense, by a reduction of reward or an increase of punishment, but they will be repaid according to the measure of their deeds that they were charged with and that their records spoke of truthfully. It has also been permitted that it be a confirmation of what precedes it regarding the imposition and recording of deeds. That is: they will not be wronged by being charged with what is not within their capacity, nor by the non-recording of some of their deeds, among which are the deeds of the moderate, on the basis that these fall short of the level of the deeds of the foremost. Rather, each of them is recorded according to its measure and its grades. The expression of the aforementioned matters as "wronging," although none of them is wronging, is in accordance with what has been established: that righteous deeds do not necessitate the basic reward, let alone necessitate a specific degree of it, so that a return with less than that would count as a deficiency. Likewise, evil deeds do not necessitate a specific degree of punishment, so that after punishment by something above it would count as an increase. Similarly, imposing what is within capacity and recording deeds are not things obligatory upon Him, glory be to Him, such that leaving them would be considered wronging, in complete glorification of the sanctity of the Glorified One from that, by depicting them in the form of what is impossible for Him, exalted is He, to do, and by naming them by His name.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 63:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, their hearts are in confusion about this﴾. It is a turning away (idrab) from what precedes it, and the pronoun refers to the disbelievers, not to everyone as in what precedes it. That is: nay, the hearts of the disbelievers are in an overwhelming heedlessness concerning this which has been explained in the Qur'an, namely that with Him, exalted is He, there is a Book that speaks with truth and makes manifest to them their evil deeds before the witnesses, whereby they will be recompensed, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He, which will come later: ﴿My verses were recited to you...﴾ and so on. It has also been said: it refers to what those described as doing righteous deeds are upon.

﴿And they have deeds﴾, many and evil, ﴿besides that﴾ (p-142), namely the aforementioned state of their hearts being in great heedlessness of what has been mentioned. These are the various kinds of their disbelief and sins, among which is their slandering of the Qur'an that will come later, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿scornfully, talking nonsense about it at night, [and] you used to revile﴾. It has also been said: it means that they surpass what the believers are described as doing of the aforementioned righteous deeds. In this there is the objection that there is no merit in describing their wicked deeds as surpassing the good deeds of the believers. It has also been said: it means that they go beyond what they are upon of polytheism, but this is far-fetched, since its mention has not preceded.

﴿They are doers of them﴾: persisting in them, accustomed to performing them, harming themselves by them, not ceasing to depart from them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 64:

﴿Until, when We seize their affluent ones with punishment﴾. That is, their pampered ones (mutrafiyhim), namely those whom Allah the Exalted provided for with the wealth and sons He has mentioned. And "until" (hatta), although it marks the endpoint (ghaya) of their aforementioned deeds, is also the starting point (mabda') for what follows from the content of the conditional clause. That is: they will keep doing their deeds up to the point where, when We seize their leaders ﴿with the punishment﴾. It has been said: it is the killing and capture on the Day of Badr. It has also been said: it is the hunger that struck them when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked against them, saying: "O Allah, make Your trampling (wati') upon Mudar severe, and make it upon them as years like the years of Joseph," so they suffered drought until they ate dogs, carrion, bones burned to ash, and children. The truth is that it is the punishment of the Hereafter, since it is that at which they are suddenly caught crying out for help and are answered with rejection and despair of victory. As for the punishment of the Day of Badr, no crying out for help was found among them at it, as the words of the Exalted indicate: ﴿And indeed We seized them with punishment, yet they did not humble themselves before their Lord, nor did they supplicate﴾, for the intended meaning of this punishment is what befell them on the Day of Badr of killing and capture, definitively. As for the punishment of hunger, although Abu Sufyan did plead with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning it, he was not answered with despair, since it is narrated that he (ﷺ) invoked for its removal and it was removed from them.

﴿Then, behold, they cry out for help﴾. That is, they suddenly began shrieking, seeking relief from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, like His words: ﴿Then to Him you cry out for help﴾, and this is the answer to the conditional. The restriction of their affluent ones to what has been mentioned, namely being seized with punishment and suddenly crying out, although the matter is general to others as well, is due to the extreme clarity of the reversal of their condition and the upending of their affairs, and because that is more grievous for them; and because, even though they were protected and guarded by the protection of others through power and retinue, when they met the terrible state they met, then those other than them among the protectors and servants are more fitting and more prone to meet it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 65:

﴿Do not cry out today﴾ is (spoken) with an implied verb of saying (ʿalā iḍmār al-qawl), coming as a rebuke to them, a reproach, and a discouragement from what they had hung their empty hopes upon, namely relief and help from His part, exalted is He. The mention of "today" specifically is to magnify its terror and to signal that they have missed the time for crying out (al-juʾār). It has been permitted that it be the response of the conditional (jawāb al-sharṭ), but you know well that the primary intent in a conditional sentence is the response, so this would result in their sudden outcry becoming not a primary intent.

As for His exalted saying: ﴿Indeed, you will not be helped by Us﴾, it is a reason (taʿlīl) for the prohibition against crying out, by showing that it is of no benefit and no use; that is, there will not reach you from Our side any help that would rescue you from what has overtaken you. It has been said: "You will not be relieved, nor will you be protected from Us." But the flow of the noble composition does not support this, because their crying out was not directed to other than Him, exalted is He, so that He would respond to them by denying that they are given victory from Him, nor does its context support it.

Indeed, His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, My verses were recited to you﴾ and so on, is clear that it is a reason (ta'lil) for what We mentioned of the non-attainment of help from His side, Exalted is He, because of their disbelief in the verses. Had the negated help been supposed to come from others, it would have been justified by their (the others') incapacity and humiliation, or by the might and power of Allah, Exalted is He. That is: ﴿My verses were recited to you﴾ in the world, ﴿so you used to turn back on your heels, retreating﴾, that is, you turned away from hearing them with the utmost aversion, let alone affirming them and acting upon them. And al-nukus (نكوص) is returning backwards (qahqara).

(Mustakbirina bihi): meaning, "proudly disdaining it," that is, [disdaining] the Sacred House (al-Bayt al-Haram) or the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram). The pronoun is said to refer to the Sacred House, because their arrogance and boasting about being its servants and custodians was well known. Or it refers to "My Book," which He described as "My verses," with istikbar (arrogance) being understood as containing the sense of takdhib (denial). Or [it refers to the Qur'an] because their arrogance toward the Muslims arose from hearing it.

It is also permissible for the preposition bi- to be connected to His words, "sāmiran" (talking nightly, as a group): that is, you would converse at night about the Qur'an and disparage it, since they used to gather around the House at night and converse (yasmurūn). The greater part of their night talk was about the Qur'an and calling it sorcery and poetry. The word sāmir is, in its usage for a group, like ḥāḍir. It has also been said that it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that came in the form of an active participle. It has been read as "samaran" and as "summaran."

The word "an" (that/in that) is connected to His words, "tahjurūn," from hajar (with a fatḥah), meaning hadhayān (raving, nonsense) or tark (abandonment): that is, you rave about the Qur'an or abandon it. Or [it is from] hajr (with a ḍammah), which means fuḥsh (obscenity/foul speech), and this is supported by the reading "tuhajirūn," from ahjara in his speech, meaning he uttered obscenity in it. It has also been read "tuhajjirūn," from hajjara, which is an intensive form of hajara meaning to rave.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 68:

﴿Will they not then ponder the word?﴾ The hamza (interrogative particle **الهَمْزَةُ**) is for denouncing the occurrence and deeming it shameful, and the fa' (**الفاءُ**) is for coordination with an implied antecedent to which the speech extends, meaning: "Do what they have done of backing away, arrogance and shunning, so that they did not ponder the Qur'an, that they might recognize, through its inimitability of composition (i'jaz al-nazm), the soundness of its meaning, and its reports of the unseen, that it is the truth from their Lord, and so believe in it, let alone what they did regarding it of ugly deeds."

And **أمْ** (am) in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Or has there come to them what did not come to their forefathers of old?﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'a), and **ما** in it carries the meaning of **بَلْ** (bal, "rather"), for turning away (idrab) and moving on (intiqal) from rebuke with what was mentioned to rebuke with another matter. The hamza is for denying the occurrence, not for denying the occurrence's reality. That is: "Rather, has there come to them of the Book what did not come to their forefathers of old, so that they found it strange and deemed it unlikely, and thus fell into what they fell into of disbelief and error?" It means that the coming of Books from Him, exalted is He, to the Messengers, peace be upon them, is an ancient practice of His, exalted is He, whose denial hardly can be sustained, and that the coming of the Qur'an in His manner is therefore: from where do they deny it?

It has also been said: "Or has there come to them, from security from His punishment, exalted is He, what did not come to their forefathers of old, such as Isma'il, peace be upon him, and his descendants from 'Adnan and Qahtan, Mudar, Rabi'a, Qiss, al-Harith ibn Ka'b, Asad ibn Khuzayma, Tamim ibn Murra, Tubba', and Dabba ibn Udd, so they believed in Him, exalted is He, and in His Books and His Messengers, and obeyed Him."

﴿Or did they not recognize their Messenger?﴾ This is a shift (idrab, a change of direction) and a transition from rebuke for what was previously mentioned to rebuke on another basis. The hamza (the interrogative particle هَمْزَة) also serves to deny that it happened, meaning: Rather, did they not recognize him (ﷺ) for his trustworthiness, truthfulness, good character, and perfect knowledge despite never having learned from anyone, and for the other perfections he possessed that befit the prophets, peace be upon them?

﴿So they are deniers of him﴾, meaning: they reject his prophethood. Their rejection of it follows from their failure to recognize his station, peace be upon him. It is necessarily the case that when the foundation is absent, what is built upon it is invalid. That is, they do not recognize him, peace be upon him, and so this is an emphasis on what precedes it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 70:

(p-144) ﴿Or do they say, "There is madness in him"?﴾ This is a transition to another rebuke. The interrogative hamza (alif of interrogation, hamzah) is for denying the reality, as in the first one; that is, "Rather, do they say there is madness (jinnah, i.e., insanity) in him," even though he is the most intelligent of people, the sharpest of mind, the most solid in judgment, and the most dignified in gravity. In these four rebukes, two of which relate to the Qur'an and the other two to him (ﷺ), the progression from the lower to the higher has been observed: they were first rebuked for not contemplating (tadabbur), which is realized even if the saying does not touch it in any way; then they were rebuked for something which, if the saying had possessed it, would have been a cause for not believing in it; then they were rebuked for what relates to the Messenger (ﷺ), namely their failure to know him (ﷺ), which is realized by not knowing good or evil; then by what, if he (ﷺ) had possessed it, would have discredited his messengership (ﷺ).

﴿Rather, he has brought them the truth﴾ This is a turning away from what the preceding indicates; that is, the matter is not as they claimed concerning the Qur'an and the Messenger (ﷺ), but rather he (ﷺ) has brought them the truth, that is, the established sincerity from which there is no deviation at all, and into which falsehood has no entry in any way.

﴿but most of them are averse to the truth﴾ Insofar as it is truth, that is, to whatever truth it may be, not merely to this particular truth, as the use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun indicates.

﴿averse﴾ Because of the crookedness and deviation in their natures that suit falsehood; for this reason they disliked this clear truth and swerved from the most evident path. Specifying "most of them" with this attribute only implies that the rest do not dislike every truth, and this does not contradict their disliking this manifest truth, so reflect. It has been said: the restriction of the judgment to "most" is because some of them abandoned faith out of disdain at being reproached by their people, or because of the weakness of their insight and their failure to reflect, not because they disliked the truth. You know well that mentioning the non-aversion of some of them to the truth, while all agree in disbelief in it, is not at all supported by the context.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 71:

﴿And if the truth had followed their desires﴾. This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) brought to explain that their deviant desires, the reason they disliked the truth was only that it did not agree with them, necessitate corruption. That is: if what they disliked of the truth, of which what the Prophet ﷺ brought is part, had been in agreement with their false desires.

﴿the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted﴾, and would have departed entirely from goodness and order, because the basis of order is nothing but that. In this there is, regarding the exalting of the status of the truth and alerting to the loftiness of its position, what is not hidden. As for what has been said: "If the truth which he ﷺ brought had followed their desires and turned into polytheism, Allah the Exalted would have brought about the Resurrection and destroyed the world, and would not have delayed," then in this is that it does not suit the supposition of his ﷺ bringing it. Likewise what has been said: "If in reality there were two gods," does not suit the context. As for what has been said: "If the truth had followed their desires, it would have gone out of divinity," this has no possibility at all.

﴿Rather, We have brought them their reminder﴾. This is a shift from censuring them for disliking the truth by which the world stands, to censuring them for turning away from what every soul has been created to desire, that in which lies its good. By "the reminder" is meant the Qur'an, which is their pride and honour, as indicated by His saying: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾. That is: rather, We have brought them their pride and honour, which they should have turned to with the utmost attentiveness.

﴿So they﴾, by what they did of recoiling ﴿from their reminder﴾, that is, their pride and honour specifically, ﴿are turning away﴾, not from other things that do not require turning to them and caring for them. The placing of the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun adds further censure and rebuke against them. The "fa'" (so) indicates that what follows, their turning away from their reminder, is consequent upon what precedes it, the bringing of their reminder, not that turning away is consequent upon bringing in general, for what entails that their turning away is a turning away from their reminder is the bringing of their reminder, not bringing in general. In attributing the bringing of the reminder to the "we" of majesty after attributing it to his pronoun ﷺ, there is an exalting of the status of the Prophet ﷺ and an alerting that it is a great station from Him, glory be to Him. In the presenting of the noble Qur'an when it is attributed to him ﷺ under the title of truth, and when it is attributed to Him, the Exalted, under the title of reminder, there is a secret subtlety and a brilliant wisdom that is not hidden, for the explicit statement of its truth, which entails the truth of the one who brought it, is what the context of relating what the falsifiers said about him requires. As for honouring, it befits Him, the Exalted, alone, especially the Messenger of Allah ﷺ being one of the honoured. It has been said: the "reminder" means what they wished for when they said, "If only we had a reminder from the earlier peoples." It has also been said: it means admonition for them, and this is supported by its having been read as "bi-dhikrahum" (with their admonition). The censure of the earlier peoples is more severe, for turning away from their admonition is not on the level of their turning away from their pride or from their reminder, which they wish for, in terms of its reprehensibility and ugliness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 72:

﴿Or do you ask them for a payment?﴾ This is a transition from rebuking them for what was mentioned in His saying: ﴿Or do they say, "There is madness in him"?﴾ to rebuking them in another way, as if it were said: Or do they claim that you ask them for a reward (kharj) for conveying the message, ﴿a payment (kharjan)﴾, that is, a wage (ju'l), and that is why they do not believe in you?

As for His exalted saying: ﴿But the payment of your Lord is better﴾, that is, His provision in this world and His reward in the Hereafter, it is a justification for the negation of asking, which is implied by the interrogative denial; that is: do not ask them for that, for what Allah the Exalted has provided you, in this world and in the next, is better for you than that. In the mention of the title "Lord" (rububiyya) together with its attribution to his pronoun (ﷺ) there is a justification of the ruling and an honouring of him (ﷺ) that is not hidden. Al-kharj corresponds to al-dakhl (income), and it is said of everything that you send out to another. Al-kharaj is predominantly used for a tax on land. It is said: al-kharj is what you give voluntarily, and al-kharaj is what is obligatory upon you. It is also said: al-kharj is more specific than al-kharaj. Thus the noble wording carries an indication of abundance and obligation. It is also read: kharjan fa-kharj, and kharajan fa-kharaj.

﴿And He is the best of providers﴾ is an affirmation of the excellence of His payment, exalted is He.

And indeed you invite them to a straight path. Sound minds bear witness to its uprightness; there is in it not the slightest trace of crookedness that could lead one to suspect you of any kind of deviation. Allah, the Mighty and Exalted, has indeed placed them under obligation and removed their pretexts in these verses, for He has enumerated the categories of what might lead to denial and accusation, and has shown that everything other than their aversion to the truth and their lack of perceptiveness has been ruled out.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 74:

﴿And indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ They are described thus as a means of censuring them for their absorption in this world and their claim that there is no life except this worldly life, and as an indication of the reason for the ruling. For belief in the Hereafter, and fear of the calamities that are in it, are among the strongest incentives to seeking the truth and following its path.

﴿from the path﴾ That is: from the kind of path ﴿are deviating﴾, i.e., they are inclined away from it, let alone from the straight path, or from the straight path to which you call them. The first is more indicative of the completeness of their error and the extremity of their misguidance, because it reveals that what they have followed is not even something that can be called a path, even if it were crooked.

﴿Had We shown them mercy and removed the harm that is upon them﴾, i.e., drought and famine, ﴿they would have persisted﴾, i.e., gone on ﴿in their transgression﴾, i.e., their excess in disbelief, arrogance, and enmity toward the Messenger ﷺ and the believers.

﴿Wandering blindly﴾, i.e., blind to guidance. It is narrated that when Thumamah ibn Uthal al-Hanafi embraced Islam, went to al-Yamamah, and prevented food supplies (al-mirah) from reaching the people of Makkah, and God afflicted them with years of famine until they ate al-'ilhiz (a food made of blood mixed with hair or wool), Abu Sufyan came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and said to him: "I beseech you by God and by kinship: do you not claim that you were sent as a mercy to the worlds?" He said: "Yes." He said: "You have killed the fathers by the sword and the sons by hunger." Then it was revealed.

The meaning is: Had We removed from them the famine and emaciation that had befallen them, by Our mercy toward them, and they found abundance, they would have returned to what they were upon of excess in disbelief and arrogance, and this humble flattery and despair would have left them. And indeed, that is how it was.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We seized them with punishment﴾ is a resumptive clause (*istiʾnāf*, a new sentence that begins afresh), brought to cite evidence for the content of the conditional clause (*sharṭiyya*). By "punishment" is meant what befell them on the Day of Badr of killing and capture, and the various kinds of punishment that befell them, of which the aforementioned famine is one. The *lām* is the answer to an omitted oath, i.e., "By God, indeed We seized them with punishment."

﴿Yet they did not humble themselves before their Lord﴾ by that, i.e., they did not submit and did not abase themselves. This verb (*istakānū*) may be either *istifʿāl* from *al-kawn* (being), because the one who submits moves from one state (*kawn*) to another, or *iftiʿāl* from *al-sukūn* (stillness), whose *fatḥa* has been lengthened, like *muntazāḥ* in *muntazaḥ*. Rather, they persisted in the insolence (*ʿutuww*) and arrogance (*istikbār*) they had been upon.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor do they supplicate﴾ is a parenthetical clause (*iʿtirāḍ*) that confirms the content of what precedes it, i.e., it is not their custom to beseech Him, exalted is He.

﴿Until, when We open upon them a gate of severe punishment﴾: this is the punishment of the Hereafter, as the awe-inspiring language of "opening a gate" and the description of it as severe indicates. It is also read as "فَتَّحْنا" (fattahna) with the doubled letter, meaning "We opened [it] wide."

﴿Behold, they will be in despair therein﴾: that is, bewildered and hopeless of every good. We afflicted them with every affliction, such as killing, captivity, hunger and other things, yet no meekness or inclination toward Islam was ever seen from them. As for what Abu Sufyan displayed, it had nothing to do with humbling themselves before God, the Exalted, or beseeching Him. It was only a kind of submissiveness until his aim was achieved. His condition is as it has been said: "When he is hungry, he whimpers, and when he is satisfied, he transgresses." Most of them persist in this state until they see the punishment of the Hereafter, and then they will be in despair.

It has also been said that the "gate" refers to hunger, for it is more severe and more comprehensive than killing and captivity. The meaning is: We first seized them with what befell them on the Day of Badr, the killing of their chieftains and their captivity, yet no supplication or humility was found among them. Then We opened upon them the gate of hunger, which is more grievous and more complete, and they were then struck with despair, their necks were humbled, and your most rebellious and most stubborn among them came to you pleading for kindness. The first view is the correct one.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 78:

﴿And it is He who produced for you hearing and sight﴾ so that you may witness through them the revealed signs (al-ayat al-tanziliyyah) and the signs of creation (al-ayat al-takwiniyyah).

﴿And hearts﴾ so that you may reflect through them upon what you witness, and draw lessons (i'tibar) of a fitting kind.

﴿Little are you grateful﴾ That is: you give little thanks, of no significant account, for those magnificent blessings, because the essence of gratitude lies in directing those faculties, which are in themselves manifest blessings, toward the purpose for which they were created; and you neglect this to a great degree.

(p-147) ﴿And it is He who multiplied you upon the earth﴾, i.e., created you and scattered you throughout it through procreation, ﴿and to Him you will be gathered﴾, i.e., you will be assembled on the Day of Resurrection after your dispersal, not to anyone else. So why do you not believe in Him and give Him thanks?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 80:

﴿And He it is Who gives life and causes death﴾, without anything among things sharing with Him in that. ﴿And His alone is﴾ ﴿the alternation of the night and the day﴾. That is: He is the One who brings about their alternation, that is, their succession, or their alternation by increase and decrease; or, by His command and decree, is their alternation.

﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ That is: will you not reflect, so that you do not use your reason? Or: will you not reflect, so that you do not use your reason, by looking and contemplating, [and realize] that the whole is from Us, and that Our power encompasses all possible things, of which the resurrection is one.

It was also read as "yaʿqilūn" (they reason), on the basis that the shift to the third person (ghayba) is to report the bad state of those addressed to others. It was said: on the basis that the first address is to include the believers by way of precedence (taghlib), but that is not so.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 81:

﴿Rather, they said﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon an implied element required by the context, meaning: "They did not reflect; rather, they said ﴿the same as what the former peoples said﴾," that is, their forefathers and those who followed their religion.

﴿They said: "When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised again?"﴾ This is an explanation of what preceded it that was ambiguous, and a detailing of what was in it by way of generality; and the discussion of it has already passed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 83:

﴿We have indeed been promised this, we and our fathers before[^1]﴾, i.e., the Resurrection (al-ba'th). ﴿Before[^1]﴾ is connected to the verb in terms of its attribution to their fathers, not to them; that is, "and our fathers were promised before," or it is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) for "our fathers," meaning: "being [promised] from before."

﴿This is nothing[^2]﴾, i.e., "this is not anything," ﴿but the fables of the ancients﴾, i.e., their lies which they inscribed (sataraha). ﴿Asatir﴾ is the plural of ﴿ustura[^3]﴾, like uhdutha (a tale) and u'juba (a marvel). It is also said that it is the plural of asfar (plural of satr, a line).

[^1]: Note: the Arabic text is the verse itself with the word "قبل" (qabl), rendered here as "before".

Translator's note: The bracketed superscripts above are not part of the original commentary; they are reserved for the glosses on technical terms and should be read as follows:
- "Ustura" (أُسْطُورَة): a fable or legend, a tale without foundation.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿Say: "To whom belongs the earth and whoever is in it, if you know?"﴾ 

"Whoever is in it" refers to created beings in general, the rational ones being given precedence over the non-rational (taghlib li-l-'uqala' 'ala ghayrihim, the predominance of rational beings over others in expression).

﴿If you know﴾: its response (jawab) is omitted, relying on the indication of the interrogative (istifham) upon it. That is, "If you know anything, then inform me of it, for that suffices as the answer." In this there is an extreme emphasis on the clarity of the matter and on declaring them ignorant, which is not hidden. Or, the meaning is: "If you know that, then inform me." In this there is contempt toward them and an affirmation of their ignorance.

Therefore He reported their answer before they gave it, saying: ﴿They will say, "To Allah."﴾ Because the immediate judgment of the intellect compels them to acknowledge that He, exalted is He, is its Creator.

﴿Say﴾, i.e., when they acknowledge this, as a rebuke to them: ﴿Will you not then take heed?﴾ i.e., do you know this, or do you say it, and yet not take heed that He who originated the earth and whatever is in it at the beginning is able to restore it a second time? For originating is not easier than restoring (p-148). Rather, the matter is the reverse according to the measure of sound reason. It is also read "tatadhakkarun" (you take heed), in its original form.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 86:

﴿Say: Whose is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?﴾ The word "Lord" (al-Rabb) is repeated to give prominence to the Throne (al-'Arsh) and to elevate its station, so that it is not made a follower of the heavens either in existence or in mention. And in the framing of the question, the progression from the lower to the higher has been observed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 87:

﴿They will say, "To Allah."﴾ With the lam (la, "to/belonging to"), taking into account the meaning of the question, for your saying "Whose is it?" (man rabbuhu) and "To whom does it belong?" (li-man huwa) have one meaning. It was also read as huwa and what follows it without the lam, taking into account the wording of the question.

﴿Say,﴾ to silence them and rebuke them, ﴿"Will you not then fear (Allah)?"﴾ That is: do you know this and yet not protect yourselves from His punishment, by not acting upon what knowledge requires, since you disbelieve in Him, deny the Resurrection, and ascribe to Him a partner in lordship (rububiyyah)?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 88:

﴿Say: "In whose hand is the dominion (malakut) of all things?"﴾ — of what has been mentioned and what has not been mentioned; that is, His complete and dominant sovereignty. It has also been said: His treasuries.

﴿And He protects, and none can be protected against Him.﴾ That is, He gives aid to others when He wills. ﴿And none can be protected against Him﴾ — that is, no one gives aid against Him, meaning no one can be prevented from Him by victory over Him.

﴿If you know﴾ — that is, something, or that; so answer Me regarding what has preceded.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 89:

﴿They will say, "To Allah."﴾ That is: to Allah belongs the dominion (malakut) of everything, and He is the One who grants protection (yujir) and against whom no protection can be granted.

﴿Say: "Then how are you deluded (tusharun)?"﴾ That is: from where are you being deceived and turned away from right guidance, despite your knowledge of it, toward what you are upon of wealth? For one who is not bewitched (masḥūr) and whose intellect is not impaired does not act in this way.

Translation:

﴿Nay, We have brought them the truth﴾ which cannot be evaded, namely monotheism (tawhid) and the promise of resurrection (al-ba'th), ﴿and indeed they are liars﴾ in what they say of polytheism (shirk) and their denial of resurrection.

﴿Allah has not taken any offspring﴾, as the Christians say, and those who say that the angels are daughters of Allah. Exalted is He far above that, with a great exaltation.

﴿Nor was there any god along with Him﴾ who shares in divinity, as the idolaters and others say.

﴿For then each god would have gone off with what he created﴾. This is the response to their argument and the consequent of a condition that has been omitted, because the preceding words indicate it. That is, if there were gods along with Him as they claim, each one of them would have gone off with what he had created, would have been independent in it, his dominion would have been distinct from the dominion of the others, and there would have arisen among them mutual domination and warfare, as is the custom among kings.

﴿And some of them would have overcome others﴾. Then no single one of them would have held the whole dominion (malakut) of everything. This is false, and no rational person has ever held it, given the established proof that all contingent beings (al-mumakkanat, i.e. possible beings) depend on one Necessary Existent (wajib al-wujud) that is one in essence.

﴿Glory be to Allah above what they describe﴾. That is, above what they attribute to Him of having rivals and offspring.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 92:

﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾, in the genitive (majrur) as an apposition (badal) to the Divine Name (al-jalalah, Allah); it has been said that it is an attributive adjective (sifah) of it. It was also read in the nominative (marfu') as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'). Whichever it is, it is another proof of the negation of a partner, on the basis that they agree that He, exalted is He, alone possesses this attribute. For this reason, His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So exalted is He above what they associate with Him﴾, is linked to it with the particle fa' (then/therefore), since His being singular in this attribute necessitates His exaltedness above having any partner.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 93:

﴿Say, "My Lord, if You should show me that which they are promised"﴾ That is: if it is necessary that You show me ﴿that which they are promised﴾ of the worldly punishment that uproots them entirely. As for the punishment of the Hereafter, the context does not suit it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 94:

﴿My Lord, do not place me among the wrongdoing people.﴾ That is: do not make me a companion to them in the punishment they are in. This implies the extreme dreadfulness of the punishment they were promised, and that it is of such a kind that one who can hardly be touched by it must seek refuge from it. It also refutes their denial of it and their hastening towards it, in the manner of mockery. It has been said that the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to say this out of humbling himself. It has also been said that it is because the evil consequences of the disbelievers may befall those who are behind them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And beware of a trial that will not afflict exclusively those among you who have done wrong.﴾ It is narrated that God, exalted is He, informed His Prophet ﷺ that there would be a punishment among his community, but did not inform him of its time, so He commanded him with this supplication and the repetition of the call. The beginning of both the condition and the response with "My Lord" is to show the utmost of supplication and earnest entreaty.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 95:

﴿And indeed We are able to show you that which We promise them﴾ of the punishment ﴿[and] indeed, We are Able﴾. But We delay it, owing to Our knowledge that some of them, or some of their descendants, will believe; or because We will not punish them while you are among them. It has been said: He has indeed shown him that, namely what befell them on the day of Badr or the conquest of Makkah. But its remoteness is not hidden, for what is immediately understood is that the punishment they deserve, which was promised, is a terrible and total annihilation, which does not appear at his hands (ﷺ), because of the wisdom that calls for it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 96:

﴿Repel evil with that which is better, [namely] forgiving it and doing good in return for it, but not in a way that leads to weakness in the religion.﴾ It was said: "That which is better" is the word of monotheism (kalimat al-tawhid), and "evil" is polytheism (shirk). It was also said: "That which is better" is enjoining what is right (al-amr bi-l-ma'ruf), and "evil" is what is wrong (al-munkar). The phrasing "repel evil with that which is better" is more emphatic than "repel the evil with the good," because it contains an explicit statement of preference (al-tafdil), and because the prepositional phrase and the object are placed first in both instances, for the sake of emphasis (li-l-ihtimam).

﴿We are most knowing of what they describe﴾, i.e., of what they attribute to you, or of their description of you as being contrary to what you are. In this there is a warning to them of recompense and punishment, a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and guidance for him (ﷺ) to entrust his affair to Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 97:

﴿And say: "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the prompting of the devils.﴾ That is: their enticing whisperings toward what is contrary to what you have been commanded of the good deeds, among which is (p-150) repelling an evil deed with a good one. The root of hamz is prodding (naskh), and from it comes mihmaz (goad) of the horse-breaker, [the metaphor being that] their urging of people toward sins is likened to the horse-breaker's goading of the animals to speed up or to leap. The plural [hamazat] is used for the repetitions [of the act], or for the variety of whisperings, or for the multiplicity of what it is attributed to.

And say, "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from their presence [ever] with me."

He (ﷺ) was commanded to seek refuge with Him, exalted is He, from their presence after he had been commanded to seek refuge from their whisperings (hamazat), for the sake of emphasis in warning against their contact. The repetition of the verb together with the repeated invocation (al-nida') serves to show the full extent of care for what is commanded and to express the utmost supplication in asking. That is: "I seek refuge in You from their coming to me and circling around me in any state whatsoever." The state of prayer and recitation of the Qur'an is singled out, as related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father), and the state of the arrival of the appointed term (ajal), as related from 'Ikrimah (may Allah have mercy on him), because these are the states most deserving of seeking refuge from them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 99:

Yet it is, along with that, a terminus for what precedes it, being connected to "they describe" (yaṣifūn), and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause (i'tirāḍ) emphasizing the overlooking (al-ighḍā') by seeking refuge in Him, exalted is He, from the devils, lest they cause him, ﷺ, to slip away from forbearance (al-ḥilm) and incite him to retaliation. But not in the sense that it is the governing element (al-'āmil) in it, because that corrupts the meaning; rather in the sense that it is an object (ma'mūl) of an elided element that is indicated by that. Its connection to "are liars" (kādhibūn) is extremely remote both verbally and in meaning, i.e., they persist in the attribute mentioned, until, when death comes to one of them, whoever he may be, the death which is inescapable for him comes and the conditions of the Hereafter become manifest to him.

﴿He says﴾ out of regret over what he neglected of faith and obedience: ﴿My Lord, send me back.﴾ That is, return me to the world. The waw (in "ir-ji'ūnī") is for honoring the one addressed. It has also been said: it is for the repetition of his saying "return me," as has been said regarding "qifā nabki" and its like.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 100:

﴿That I may do righteous deeds in what I have left behind.﴾ That is: concerning the faith that I have left behind, he did not arrange it within the category of hope, as with the other righteous deeds, by saying: "Perhaps I will believe and then act..." etc. This is to indicate that it is a matter whose occurrence is decided, needing no report of its certain occurrence, let alone that it is hoped to occur. That is: "Perhaps I will act, in the faith that I have brought, a righteous deed, absolutely." It was also said: "in what I have left behind" refers to wealth or to the worldly life. And from him ﷺ: "When the believer sees the angels, they say: 'Shall we return you to the world?' He says: 'To the house of worries and sorrows? ﴿Not so!﴾ This is a rebuke against asking for a return and a declaring it far-fetched. ﴿Indeed, it is⦅ that⦆﴾ That is: his saying "My Lord, send me back" etc. ﴿a word he is saying⦅ only⦆﴾ without doubt, since regret has taken hold of him.

﴿And before them⦅ is⦆﴾ That is: in front of them. The pronoun refers to one of them, and the plural is by consideration of meaning, since it carries the ruling of all of them, just as the singular in the earlier pronouns is by consideration of wording.

﴿Then as for those whose scales are heavy﴾: "Mawzunat" (the weighed things) of their good deeds, from the beliefs and the actions; that is, whoever has sound beliefs ('aqa'id) and righteous deeds, these will have weight and standing (wazn wa-qadr) with Allah the Exalted.

﴿Those are the ones who will be successful﴾: the ones who attain every sought-after goal and are saved from every feared thing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 103:

﴿And as for those whose scales are light﴾, i.e., whoever has no beliefs or deeds that carry any weight or value in His sight, and they are the disbelievers, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We shall not assign them any weight on the Day of Resurrection﴾. The detailed discussion of what pertains to this matter has already passed in the tafsir of (Surat al-A'raf).

﴿Those are the ones who have lost their souls﴾: they destroyed them by squandering the time for their perfection, and they nullified their readiness to attain their perfection. The demonstrative noun (ism al-ishara) in both places is an expression for the relative pronoun (al-mawsul), and its plural form is used in consideration of its meaning, just as the singular form of the two pronouns in the relative clauses (al-silatan) is used in consideration of its wording.

﴿Abiding in Hell﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for the relative clause, or a second predicate (khabar thani) for ﴿those﴾.

﴿وَهم فِيها كالِحُونَ﴾ (and they therein are grim-faced), from the severity of the burning. Al-kulūh (kulūḥ) is the drawing back of the two lips from the teeth. It has also been read as "kalihūn" (kalihūn).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 105:

﴿Were not My verses recited to you?﴾ This is by supposing an implied saying (ʿalā iḍmār al-qawl), meaning: it is said to them, as rebuke, reproach, and reminder of what made them deserve the punishment with which they were afflicted: "Were not My verses recited to you in the world?" ﴿Then you used to deny them﴾ at that time.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 106:

﴿They said: "Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us"﴾ i.e., it took possession of us, ﴿our wretchedness﴾ which we incurred through our own evil choice, as is indicated by its being attributed to themselves (anfusihim). ﴿And we were﴾ because of that ﴿a people astray﴾ from the truth; for that reason we did what we did of denial. And this, as you see, is an acknowledgement from them that what befell them had befallen them through their own wrongdoing.

As for what has been said, that it is an excuse offered by them, citing the overpowering of the eternal wretchedness that was decreed for them, then, although it is false in itself, since nothing of happiness and wretchedness is decreed for them except what God, exalted is He, knows they will do by their own choice, because knowledge follows the known, it is refuted by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it, and if we return, then indeed we are wrongdoers﴾. That is, bring us out of the Fire and send us back to the world, and if we return after that to what we were upon of disbelief and sins, then indeed we are transgressing the limit in wrongdoing. Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 111:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I have rewarded them today﴾ is a resumption (isti'naf) to explain the goodness of their state and that they have benefited from what they endured of harm from you.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 112:

﴿Said﴾ — i.e., Allah, mighty and majestic, or the angel commanded with that, as a reminder of how long they remained, concerning which they asked to return to the world, after the warning about its impossibility by His saying: ﴿"Begone into it, and do not speak to Me."﴾ etc. It was also read as "Say" (qul) in the imperative, addressed to the angel.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 115:

﴿Did you think that We created you without purpose?﴾ That is: Do you not know anything, so that you thought that We created you without a perfect wisdom, to the extent that you denied the Resurrection? Here "ʿabathan" (in vain, without purpose) is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the "nūn" of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓama, the plural of greatness in "We"), meaning: playing or trifling. Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 116:

﴿So exalted is Allah﴾ — an expression of magnifying Him, may He be exalted, for His affairs by which His servants are dealt with: origination and return, reward and punishment, in accordance with perfect wisdom. ﴿The King, the Truth﴾ — the One to whom sovereignty belongs absolutely, in bringing into being and annihilation, in beginning and return, in giving life and causing death, in punishment and reward. Everything other than Him is owned by Him and subdued beneath His dominion (malakut).

﴿There is no god but Him﴾ — for everything else besides Him is His servant. ﴿Lord of the Noble Throne﴾ — so how much more so of what is beneath it and encompassed by it of existent things, whatever they may be. Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 23, verse 117:

﴿And whoever calls upon another god along with Allah﴾ worships him, both individually and in association (with Allah). ﴿for which he has no proof﴾ is a necessary attribute (ṣifah lāzimah) of "ilāhan" (another god), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿flies with its two wings﴾. It was brought for emphasis, and for building the ruling upon it, as an alert that adhering to a religion for which there is no evidence is void; so how much more so for that which the immediate judgment of minds testifies against. Or it is an interjection (i'tirāḍ) between the conditional and its response, like your saying: "Whoever does good to Zayd, there is no one more deserving of goodness than him, so Allah will reward him."

﴿Then his reckoning is only with his Lord﴾: so He will recompense him according to what he deserves. ﴿Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed﴾: that is, indeed the matter is... etc. It has also been read with a fatḥah (innahu), on the basis that it is a causal clause (taʿlīl), or a predicate (khabar), and its meaning is: his reckoning is the non-success (of such a person). The original is: his reckoning is that he will not succeed, he himself; so "the disbelievers" was placed in the position of the pronoun, because "man yadʿu" (whoever calls) carries the meaning of the plural. Likewise, "ḥisābuhu annahu lā yufliḥu" carries the meaning of "ḥisābuhum annahum lā yufliḥūn" (their reckoning is that they will not succeed).

The noble surah began by affirming the success of the believers and ended by denying success to the disbelievers. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was commanded to seek forgiveness and mercy, and it was said: ﴿And say: "My Lord, forgive and have mercy, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾ This indicates that these two are among the most important religious matters, since the one commanded to do so, whose past and future sins had been forgiven, is the Prophet (ﷺ). How much more so is it for anyone else?

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Mu'minun (The Believers), the angels will give him good news of rest (al-rawh), sweet basil (al-rayhan), and that which will delight his eye at the arrival of the Angel of Death." And from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Ten verses have been revealed to me; whoever upholds them will enter Paradise." Then he recited: "Successful indeed are the believers," until he finished the ten.

It is also narrated that "its first part and its last part are treasures of Paradise: whoever acts upon three verses from its beginning and takes admonition from four from its end has indeed been saved and succeeded."
